R/classify_esrd_causes.R sits in main.R after download_public_data.R as a commented-out line: it calls paid APIs, so an authorized person runs it once by hand. From the public $PD96DET code list it writes the three references/ files in its row above; the deciders review the mapping, and link_area_data.R reads only that reviewed file. Which models vote, the agreement rule, saved answers and the safeguards for the review are described on its site page.

Key mechanisms

Labels from the source documentation. usRds::load_usrds_file() and apply_usrds_factors() turn USRDS codes into their Appendix C meanings. Filters compare against those labels (for example DIALSET %in% dialysis_settings_kept). PDIS is kept as the raw code for the cause mapping.
Facility counts by date. usRds::add_dialysis_facility_counts() matches each patient’s DIALDAT to the CMS release in effect (an interval join on valid_from/valid_to), then counts facilities in the ZIP code and in its HSA for that calendar year. Rows never multiply; dates outside coverage give NA.
Cohort and diagram from one object. Every exclusion is an fc_filter() call on linked_forms; cohort is fc_view(cohort_fc, what = "data"). No script removes patients elsewhere. fc_filter() re-evaluates each condition as text, so conditions use only columns and global constants.
Joins state their relationship. Every join of area data to patients is many-to-one; a duplicate key stops the run.
ZIP codes reach ACS through ZCTAs. Each ZIP code is mapped to its ZCTA with the UDS Mapper crosswalk for the year dialysis started (zippeR); HSA population counts each ZCTA once (hsa_population_from_zcta()).
Public inputs are checked. ACS labels are checked for every year (check_acs_labels()); Dartmouth columns are found by pattern and must match exactly one column (select_by_pattern()).
Cause codes. link_area_data.R reads code and final_category from the mapping, stops if a code lacks one of the six categories, and warns with the share of first forms whose cause code is not in the mapping; those count as Other.
Published models from one list. models.R builds published_models, one row per published table, block and model; models shared between blocks are fit once (by a hash of their specification) with glmmTMB, and imputed models are pooled across the completed data sets. The variance decomposition fits two null linear mixed models of eGFR with lme4::lmer() (HSA, and facility nested in HSA) on the same patients, those with a facility ID, and variance_shares() turns each into shares of variance.

Dependencies outside this repository

usRds: needs the version containing dialysis_facility_snapshots, add_dialysis_facility_counts() and summarize_dialysis_facilities(), which is under review in the usRds project. R/classify_esrd_causes.R reads the internal usRds:::metadata_c until the package exports its format tables.
Packages used without being attached: ellmer, irr and rlang (classification), broom.mixed (estimates).
Census API key for tidycensus; API keys for OpenAI, Anthropic and Google, and Ollama with the two local models, for the one-time classification.

Website
_quarto.yml and index.qmd at the root; one page per definitive script in quarto/, plus background, differences, results, supplement, the original file and about. Four pages show the project documents (analysis-plan.qmd, architecture.qmd, agents.qmd, repository-blueprint.qmd); each only includes its file from the repository root, which stays the one source, so the plan’s citations resolve on the site. Pages import code from R/ with knitr::read_chunk() and never evaluate it. Helpers used only by the pages are in quarto/_site_functions.R: side_by_side_diff() for before-and-after code comparisons, and rmd_as_markdown(), which shows the original R Markdown file on its page as formatted text with each chunk folded, without running anything. Their style is in styles.css, and main.R never sources them. The site renders to docs/, which is not committed: .github/workflows/publish.yml renders it on every pull request as a check and, on each push to main, renders it and publishes it to the gh-pages branch, which GitHub Pages serves.

Tests
tests/test-functions.R tests the helpers in R/functions.R on synthetic data with known answers, including the classification helpers with fake provider functions in place of the models. Two helpers are not tested there: read_header_table(), and map_panel(), which is checked by the synthetic run of figures.R. density_category_labels() is tested through categorize_density(), which uses it to name the five density categories. format_estimates_table() is tested only where gt is installed. tests/test-model-example.R checks that the model written out on the models page is the one the code fits for Table 2, Model 3, using only constants from setup.R. tests/test-site-functions.R tests the site helpers. tests/check-crosslinks.R is not a test file but a check the publish workflow runs on every pull request: it reads the scripts and the pages and fails if the functions page and the method pages do not link each other as the code says.

title: 2. Cause of kidney failure
text: Drafts the mapping of every USRDS primary-cause code to the six categories of the paper’s Table 1, using three cloud large language models. Codes on which at least two of the three agree are accepted without being read by a person; the deciders review the rest. Two smaller models that run on the analyst’s own computer answer the same question and are reported for comparison, but do not vote: neither produced a complete, valid set of answers (see What the local models showed). The mapping from the first full run, on 30 October 2026, is accepted for the replication as the models drafted it (decided by Vagish Hemmige, 30 October 2026; decision D4): 423 of the 445 codes were unanimous and 22 accepted by two of three, none were left for review, and the deciders changed none. This step comes after the public area data and before any USRDS data are loaded, and it uses none. Its line in R/main.R is commented out: the script is run once, by hand, because it calls paid APIs and needs the local models, and the file it writes to references/ is what the analysis reads once the deciders have reviewed it.

title: 2. Cause of kidney failure
text:
ellmer version
ellmer asks Claude for its native structured output only for model names it recognizes, and it recognizes Claude 5 names such as claude-sonnet-5-5 from version 0.5.0 (the function has_claude_structured_output() in ellmer’s source). Older versions force a tool call instead, which current Claude models reject with the error “tool_choice … not supported for this model”.


Click to show/hide R Code
# ellmer sends Claude a native structured-output request only for model names
# it recognizes; Claude 5 names (such as claude-sonnet-5-5) are recognized from
# ellmer 0.5.0 (has_claude_structured_output() in R/provider-claude.R). Older
# versions force a tool call instead, which current Claude models reject
# ("tool_choice ... not supported for this model").
if (packageVersion("ellmer") < "0.5.0") {
  stop(str_glue(
    "ellmer {packageVersion('ellmer')} is too old for the Claude model in setup.R. ",
    "Run install.packages(\"ellmer\") to get 0.5.0 or later."
  ), call. = FALSE)
}

title: 2. Cause of kidney failure
2. Cause of kidney failure
2. Cause of kidney failure
text:
The prompt
All five models, voting or not, receive the same prompt, word for word. It is kept as a text file, prompts/esrd-cause-classification.md, so that it can be read and edited on its own and shown here exactly as sent:
You are a nephrologist classifying the primary cause of kidney failure recorded on the CMS-2728 Medical Evidence form, using the USRDS code list.

Assign each code to exactly one of these categories:

- Diabetes: kidney failure attributed to type 1 or type 2 diabetes, including diabetic nephropathy and diabetes with renal manifestations.
- Hypertension and cardiac disease: hypertensive kidney disease and nephrosclerosis, hypertensive heart and kidney disease, renovascular and other large-vessel disease of the kidney (renal artery stenosis, occlusion or thrombosis, renal atheroembolism), and kidney failure attributed to heart disease, such as cardiorenal syndrome or heart failure.
- Glomerulonephritis: primary and secondary glomerular disease. Primary includes IgA nephropathy, focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, membranous nephropathy, membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis, and acute, rapidly progressive or chronic nephritic and nephrotic syndromes. Secondary includes glomerulonephritis caused by systemic disease: lupus nephritis, ANCA-associated vasculitis (granulomatosis with polyangiitis or Wegener's granulomatosis, microscopic polyangiitis, polyarteritis), anti-GBM disease (Goodpasture's syndrome) and Henoch-Schönlein purpura. It also includes infection-related glomerular disease: post-infectious glomerulonephritis, HIV-associated (AIDS) nephropathy, glomerulonephritis associated with hepatitis B or C, and cryoglobulinemic glomerulonephritis. Thrombotic microangiopathies (hemolytic-uremic syndrome, thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura), scleroderma, and lupus described as tubulointerstitial disease are not in this category.
- Hereditary or polycystic kidney disease: polycystic kidney disease and other inherited kidney diseases, including medullary cystic disease, Alport syndrome, Fabry disease, cystinosis, primary oxalosis and tuberous sclerosis. Congenital anomalies that are not described as inherited (renal hypoplasia or dysplasia, congenital obstruction) are not in this category.
- Transplant failure or complications: complications or failure of any transplanted solid organ or of bone marrow.
- Other: any cause that fits none of the five categories above. This includes:
  - other kidney and urinary tract disease: interstitial nephritis, pyelonephritis and other kidney or urinary tract infections (including renal tuberculosis), obstructive and urologic disease, congenital anomalies that are not inherited, and acute kidney injury;
  - systemic disease that is not glomerulonephritis: thrombotic microangiopathies, scleroderma, neoplasms (including myeloma and amyloidosis);
  - codes meaning that the cause is missing, unknown or unreconcilable.

Classify from the code and its description only; do not assume information that is not given.
Return one entry per code, with the code exactly as given and a reason of at most 15 words.

Codes:
{{code_list}}
For each batch, {code_list} becomes one line per code: the code, a colon and the USRDS description from the Researcher’s Guide (for example, 4464Z: WEGENERS GRANULOMATOSIS). Nothing else about a code is sent. The script stops if the prompt does not define each of the six categories, under exactly the names in setup.R, because the structured output can only return those names.
The prompt makes three rules:

One category per code, from the six in the paper’s Table 1, each defined in words.
“Other” is the catch-all, for every cause outside the first five and for codes that mean missing, unknown or unreconcilable. This is an assumption: the original spreadsheet had a sheet named “Other”, but what it contained is not known.
No inference beyond the description. The model classifies from the code and its description only, which keeps it from inventing context.

title: 2. Cause of kidney failure
text:
The six categories
The original analysis took the six categories from a spreadsheet with one sheet per category (“Diabetes”, “Hypertensive and Cardiac”, “Glomerulonephritis”, “HereditaryPCKD”, “Transplant”, “Other”), which no longer exists. Only the categories’ names survive, in the sheet names and in the paper’s Table 1, which labels the transplant category “solid organ and bone marrow” (Hemmige et al. 2024).
The definitions in the prompt (decided by Vagish Hemmige, 27 October 2026) start from the 12 headings of the 2015 CMS-2728 list of primary causes (Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services 2015) and depart from them where the clinical definition differs:







CMS-2728 heading (2015)
Category here




Diabetes
Diabetes


Glomerulonephritis
Glomerulonephritis


Secondary Glomerulonephritis/Vasculitis
Glomerulonephritis for lupus nephritis, ANCA vasculitis and Henoch-Schönlein purpura; Other for thrombotic microangiopathies (hemolytic-uremic syndrome, thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura) and scleroderma


Interstitial Nephritis/Pyelonephritis
Other


Transplant Complications
Transplant failure or complications


Hypertension/Large Vessel Disease
Hypertension and cardiac disease


Cystic/Hereditary/Congenital/Other Diseases
Hereditary or polycystic kidney disease for cystic and inherited disease; Other for congenital anomalies not described as inherited


Neoplasms/Tumors
Other


Disorders of Mineral Metabolism
Other


Genitourinary System
Other


Acute Kidney Failure
Other


Miscellaneous Conditions
Other, except heart failure (Hypertension and cardiac disease) and HIV disease (Glomerulonephritis)



The 2015 list covers only the ICD-10-CM codes. The older ICD-9-CM codes in $PD96DET are placed by the same definitions; anti-GBM disease (Goodpasture’s syndrome), for example, appears only among them and counts as glomerulonephritis.
Four departures need a reason:

Secondary glomerulonephritis is glomerulonephritis. The CMS list keeps it apart, but lupus nephritis, ANCA vasculitis and Henoch-Schönlein purpura are glomerular inflammation. Lupus described as tubulointerstitial disease is not, and goes to Other. Thrombotic microangiopathies and scleroderma kidney disease, in the same CMS heading, are injury to the small vessels and endothelium rather than glomerular inflammation, so they also go to Other.
Infection-related glomerular disease is glomerulonephritis: post-infectious glomerulonephritis, glomerulonephritis with hepatitis B or C, and cryoglobulinemic glomerulonephritis. Infections that are not glomerular, such as pyelonephritis and renal tuberculosis, stay in Other.
HIV-associated nephropathy is glomerulonephritis. The 2015 CMS list places HIV disease (code B20) under Miscellaneous Conditions (Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services 2015). Clinically, HIV-associated nephropathy is a glomerular disease whose classic form is collapsing focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (Rosenberg et al. 2015), so here it counts as glomerulonephritis, a deliberate departure from the CMS grouping. On the first run, before the definitions were written, all three models put HIV in Other. Earlier versions of the prompt are in the repository’s history, and each saved answer file names the prompt version it answered.
Heart failure is cardiac disease. The sheet name “Hypertensive and Cardiac” suggests that kidney failure attributed to heart disease belonged with hypertension, so heart failure (I50.9, in Miscellaneous Conditions on the CMS list) counts there.

Transplant failure or complications. The paper’s Table 1 labels this category “solid organ and bone marrow”. On a first Medical Evidence form it mostly means kidney failure after a transplant of another organ (heart, liver, lung) or of bone marrow, for example from calcineurin-inhibitor toxicity. A failed kidney transplant would not usually start incident dialysis, since that patient already had kidney failure.
What the paper’s Table 1 can and cannot show. In the published cohort, the six categories were diabetes 48.0%, hypertension and cardiac disease 29.5%, glomerulonephritis 5.7%, hereditary or polycystic kidney disease 1.9%, transplant 0.5% and other 14.3% (computed from the Table 1 counts). Among all incident patients in 2016, glomerulonephritis was 7.3% and cystic kidney disease 2.8% (computed from the counts in Table 1.6 of the 2018 USRDS Annual Data Report (United States Renal Data System 2018)). The cohort is in-center hemodialysis only, and patients with glomerulonephritis or cystic kidney disease more often start on peritoneal dialysis or receive a transplant first (Table 1.6 (United States Renal Data System 2018)), so these percentages cannot show where the original spreadsheet drew either boundary. Small groups such as HIV are invisible in these percentages.

title: 2. Cause of kidney failure
2. Cause of kidney failure
text:
One function per model
Five models, set in setup.R, three voting and two reported, all called through ellmer (Wickham et al., n.d.) with the same structured output. Each model has its own function, so each can be run, checked and saved on its own. Claude’s answers are capped at 4,096 tokens by default in ellmer, too few for 100 codes with reasons, so its limit is raised (esrd_classifier_claude_max_tokens).
The three cloud models are each provider’s current general-purpose model. The two local models run through Ollama on the analyst’s computer (decided by Vagish Hemmige, 28 October 2026): Alibaba’s Qwen and Meta’s Llama, from two further companies. They were chosen to vote, and were moved to reporting only on 29 October 2026 (decided by Vagish Hemmige), when neither produced a complete, valid set of answers. Qwen answers with its “thinking” turned off (reasoning_effort = "none"): with it on, its reasoning filled Ollama’s working space before it wrote the answer, and the answer was cut off. Llama 3.1 replaced IBM’s Granite (granite4.2:8b) on 29 October 2026 (decided by Vagish Hemmige): on the analyst’s laptop Granite timed out after 30 minutes on a batch of 25 codes, and returned no answers for 5 codes in 15 minutes. Ollama’s models trained for medicine were considered, but they are all Google’s MedGemma, which would overlap with Gemini, or older models built on Llama 2. Both local models are small enough to run on a laptop. They show the approach that would be needed if a classification ever involved patient data: a model on the analyst’s own computer sends nothing to an outside company. Here only the public code list is used, so the cloud models are allowed, and the local models show what that approach costs.


Click to show/hide R Code
# One function per model. Each takes a batch of codes and returns one row per
# code with code, category and reason, through ellmer's structured output.
# Each call starts a new chat, so no batch sees another batch's answers.
ask_openai <- function(batch) {
  chat <- ellmer::chat_openai(model = esrd_classifier_models$openai, echo = "none")
  chat$chat_structured(classification_prompt(batch), type = classification_type)
}

ask_google <- function(batch) {
  chat <- ellmer::chat_google_gemini(model = esrd_classifier_models$google, echo = "none")
  chat$chat_structured(classification_prompt(batch), type = classification_type)
}

ask_anthropic <- function(batch) {
  chat <- ellmer::chat_anthropic(
    model = esrd_classifier_models$anthropic,
    params = ellmer::params(max_tokens = esrd_classifier_claude_max_tokens),
    echo = "none"
  )
  chat$chat_structured(classification_prompt(batch), type = classification_type)
}

# The two local models run through Ollama (http://localhost:11434), in the
# same way; ask_ollama() returns the function for one of them, with any
# settings it needs (passed to ellmer::params())
ask_ollama <- function(model, ...) {
  function(batch) {
    chat <- ellmer::chat_ollama(model = model, params = ellmer::params(...), echo = "none")
    chat$chat_structured(classification_prompt(batch), type = classification_type)
  }
}

providers <- list(
  openai = ask_openai,
  anthropic = ask_anthropic,
  google = ask_google,
  # Qwen's "thinking" off (see setup.R)
  ollama_qwen = ask_ollama(esrd_classifier_models$ollama_qwen, reasoning_effort = "none"),
  ollama_llama = ask_ollama(esrd_classifier_models$ollama_llama)
)

# A local model on a laptop processor can take longer than ellmer's default
# wait of 5 minutes per answer
options(ellmer_timeout_s = esrd_classifier_timeout_s)

title: 2. Cause of kidney failure
text:
Setting up Ollama
Ollama runs open-weight models on the analyst’s own computer, and ellmer talks to it with chat_ollama(). Its advantage is privacy: in Ollama’s words, “Ollama runs locally. We don’t see your prompts or data when you run locally” (Ollama FAQ). A cloud model, by contrast, receives every prompt on the provider’s servers. This step sends only the public code list, so the cloud models are allowed here, and the local models are a demonstration of the approach that text containing patient information would need. Whether a particular computer and setup are acceptable for protected health information is for the institution to decide, not something Ollama guarantees.
Two cautions about the privacy claim:

Ollama also offers cloud models, run on Ollama’s servers, and its cloud features are on by default. The models used here are local, but to rule out sending anything by mistake, Ollama can run in local-only mode: set the environment variable OLLAMA_NO_CLOUD=1 and restart Ollama; its log then shows Ollama cloud disabled: true (Ollama FAQ: disabling cloud features).
The models are downloaded from the internet (ollama pull), and Ollama checks for its own updates. Only the prompts and answers stay on the computer.

The disadvantage is setup. Ollama has to be installed, the models downloaded (5–8 GB each), and Ollama has to find a way to run them that works on that computer. On a computer without a capable graphics card the models run on the processor, which is much slower than the cloud models.

Steps

Install Ollama from ollama.com/download. The Windows notes give the requirements and where Ollama keeps its files.
Download the two models in a terminal: ollama pull qwen3.5:9b and ollama pull llama3.1:8b (Qwen 3.5, Llama 3.1). On a computer with less memory, qwen3.5:4b (3–4 GB) is a smaller choice; change its name in setup.R.
Test each model in the terminal before running the script: ollama run qwen3.5:9b "Say hello". A model that cannot answer this will not answer the script either, and the terminal shows the error directly.
Measure the speed: ollama run qwen3.5:9b --verbose "Say hello" prints, after the answer, an eval rate in tokens per second. A batch of 25 codes needs roughly 1,000 tokens of answer, so at 5 tokens per second a batch takes about 3 minutes and the 18 batches about an hour, per model. The first request after starting Ollama also loads the model from disk, which takes up to a minute. Qwen 3.5 “thinks” before it answers, which adds to the time (Ollama: thinking).



If a model crashes: the graphics card
Ollama looks for a graphics card and puts as much of the model on it as fits. If the card or its driver is not up to it, the model crashes while loading, and every model fails, including the smallest. This happened on the computer used for this project on 28 October 2026, a Windows laptop with an Intel Core i7-8850H, 32 GB of memory and a small NVIDIA Quadro P1000 graphics card (4 GB) beside the processor’s built-in graphics:

With Ollama 0.40.4 and 0.40.12, every model crashed with exit status 0xc0000005. The log showed the model being loaded onto CUDA0, the NVIDIA card.
Hiding the card from CUDA (below) made a different error appear, exit status 0xe06d7363. The log showed Ollama then using the same card through Vulkan, another way of reaching graphics cards, and ggml_vulkan: device lost on Vulkan0.
Turning off both made every model run, on the processor only.

Ollama’s hardware page says that NVIDIA cards of this generation (compute capability 5.0 to 6.2) need driver version 570 or newer, and the log reported a driver supporting CUDA 12.2, which points to an older driver. Updating the driver was not tried; the 4 GB card would hold only a small part of these models in any case.
To run on the processor only (Windows; type in a terminal, then quit Ollama from its icon by the clock, start it again, and open a new terminal):
setx CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES -1
setx OLLAMA_VULKAN 0
Both come from Ollama’s hardware page: an invalid card number such as -1 makes Ollama ignore NVIDIA cards, and OLLAMA_VULKAN=0 turns off Vulkan. CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES also hides the NVIDIA card from any other program that uses CUDA (machine-learning software, for example), though not from the screen, video or games. To undo either, delete it under “Edit environment variables for your account” in Windows (Ollama FAQ: environment variables on Windows).
Reading Ollama’s log. On Windows the logs are in %LOCALAPPDATA%\Ollama (paste that into the Windows Run box, Windows key + R); server.log is the newest and server-1.log and so on are older (Ollama troubleshooting). The lines that matter:

inference compute, near the start: what Ollama will use. library=cpu means the processor; library=CUDA or Vulkan means a graphics card.
load_tensors: ... model buffer size, when a model loads: where it was put (CPU, CUDA0, Vulkan0).
The last lines before Load failed: the actual error.

In a terminal, powershell -command "Get-Content $env:LOCALAPPDATA\Ollama\server.log -Tail 60" shows the end of the log.

section: Running, checking and saving each model

title: 2. Cause of kidney failure
text:
Agreement
A code is accepted when at least two of the three cloud models agree, a majority rule chosen for this demonstration (decided by Vagish Hemmige, 29 October 2026; the rule was three of five while the local models voted). Accepted codes are not read by a person. agreement says, for each code, whether the models were unanimous, how many agreed (for example “2 of 3 models”), or that no category had a majority. For codes with no majority, the deciders fill final_category and their initials in reviewer.
Fleiss’ kappa describes how far the models agree beyond chance: 1 is perfect agreement and 0 is what chance alone would give. It is reported in the agreement summary, and is not used to accept or reject codes.
Functions used: ensemble_agreement().


Click to show/hide R Code
mapping <- ensemble_agreement(votes, cause_codes, min_agreement = esrd_classifier_min_agreement) |>
  mutate(
    final_category = model_category,
    agreement = case_when(
      unanimous ~ "unanimous",
      !is.na(model_category) ~ str_glue("{n_agreeing} of {n_providers} models"),
      .default = "no majority"
    ),
    # Filled by the deciders for every code they review
    reviewer = NA_character_,
    prompt_version = prompt_version,
    ellmer_version = as.character(packageVersion("ellmer")),
    models = str_flatten(unlist(esrd_classifier_models[esrd_classifier_voting]), "; "),
    mapping_written_on = as.character(Sys.Date())
  )

# Fleiss' kappa describes how far the models agree beyond chance
# (1 = perfect, 0 = chance). It is reported, not used to accept codes.
kappa <- mapping |>
  select(starts_with("category_")) |>
  irr::kappam.fleiss()

agreement_summary <- tibble(
  codes = nrow(mapping),
  unanimous = sum(mapping$agreement == "unanimous"),
  majority_only = sum(!is.na(mapping$model_category) & mapping$agreement != "unanimous"),
  no_majority = sum(is.na(mapping$model_category)),
  fleiss_kappa = kappa$value,
  kappa_z = kappa$statistic,
  kappa_p_value = kappa$p.value,
  prompt_version = prompt_version,
  models = first(mapping$models),
  written_on = as.character(Sys.Date())
)

message(str_glue(
  "{agreement_summary$unanimous} of {agreement_summary$codes} codes unanimous, ",
  "{agreement_summary$majority_only} by majority only, ",
  "{agreement_summary$no_majority} with no majority; ",
  "Fleiss' kappa {round(agreement_summary$fleiss_kappa, 3)}. ",
  "Review the codes with no majority before running main.R."
))

title: 2. Cause of kidney failure
text:
What the local models showed
The two local models were meant to vote, and were run on the analyst’s laptop (processor only, 32 GB of memory) on 28 and 29 October 2026. Neither produced a complete, valid set of answers, so neither votes (decided by Vagish Hemmige, 29 October 2026); their answers are kept and reported, because what they did is itself a finding of this demonstration.

They dropped codes in longer batches. Both answered every code of a 5-code test. In batches of 25, Qwen left 150 of the 445 codes unanswered even after asking a second time, and Llama answered 7 of a 25-code test. Even in batches of 5, Llama left 124 codes unanswered on its first pass, and 28 after asking a second time.
They returned text that is not a code. Qwen put 25 codes in quotation marks and returned one answer with no code. Llama returned codes with </code> attached, the placeholders {code} and What is the code?, four invented web addresses, and codes not in the list (for example Z88.0, and D1022 for E1022). In all, 20 of its answers carried text that is not a code in the list, and it answered 6 codes more than once, some with different categories.
Some categories contradict the model’s own reason or are clinically wrong. Qwen put AIDS nephropathy (429) under Diabetes, with the reason that it “falls under viral/glomerular causes … not diabetes”. Llama put lupus nephritis (7100) and membranous nephropathy (5831) under Diabetes, and malignant hypertension (4010) under Diabetes with the reason “No indication of diabetes”.
They were slow. Qwen took 108 minutes for its answers; Llama about 2.5 minutes per batch of 5, close to four hours for the list. The cloud models took minutes.
A third model did not run at all. IBM’s Granite (granite4.2:8b) timed out after 30 minutes on a batch of 25 codes, and returned no answers for 5 codes in 15 minutes; Llama replaced it.

These are observations from one laptop and one prompt, not a general verdict on local models; larger local models, a computer with a capable graphics card, or a prompt asking for fewer codes at a time might do better. references/esrd-cause-local-models.csv records, for each local model, how many codes it answered once with a code from the list, left unanswered or answered with other text, and how often it gave the category the cloud models accepted (local_model_report(), on the functions page).
Functions used: local_model_report().


Click to show/hide R Code
# How complete and valid each local model's answers were, and how often it
# agreed with the category the voting models accepted
local_report <- all_votes |>
  filter(!provider %in% esrd_classifier_voting) |>
  local_model_report(cause_codes, accepted = mapping) |>
  mutate(
    model = unlist(esrd_classifier_models[provider]),
    prompt_version = prompt_version,
    written_on = as.character(Sys.Date()),
    .after = provider
  )

message(str_glue_data(
  local_report,
  "{provider}: {codes_answered} of {nrow(cause_codes)} codes answered once, ",
  "{codes_missing} missing, {answers_not_in_list} answers not in the list; ",
  "agreed with {agrees_with_accepted} of {compared_with_accepted} accepted categories."
))

title: 2. Cause of kidney failure
text:
How the mapping is checked
Agreement among the models shows only that they agree, not that they are right. The plan adds two checks on the data, run by an authorized person once the mapping is reviewed:

Against USRDS’s own grouping. The USRDS PATIENTS file carries a primary disease group for each patient (DISGRPC). A cross-tabulation of the six categories against it, as percentages with small cells suppressed, shows which codes the mapping puts somewhere USRDS does not. Differences are expected where the definitions depart from the CMS grouping on purpose (secondary glomerulonephritis, HIV, heart failure); any others point to codes to review.
Against the paper. The cohort’s share in each category, compared with the published Table 1 percentages above. A large gap in one category points to codes to review.

title: Setup
text: This script attaches every package the analysis uses and defines every constant a reader might want to change. Other scripts never call library() or hard-code a number.

title: Setup
text:
Packages
Each data source has an access package: usRds for the USRDS files and the CMS facility snapshots, tidycensus for the American Community Survey. flowchart builds the cohort, so the STROBE diagram and the analytic data come from the same code. glmmTMB fits the mixed-effects logistic models and lme4 the linear ones, gtsummary and gt build the tables, and mice imputes albumin and hemoglobin.


Click to show/hide R Code
library(tidyverse)
library(labelled)
library(usRds)        # USRDS files, value labels, CMS facility snapshots
library(flowchart)    # cohort flow: every exclusion is an fc_filter() step
library(tidycensus)   # American Community Survey (needs a Census API key)
library(zippeR)       # ZIP code to ZCTA crosswalks by year (UDS Mapper)
library(readxl)
library(sf)
library(lme4)        # linear mixed models (eGFR as a continuous outcome)
library(glmmTMB)     # mixed-effects logistic models
library(broom.mixed)
library(gtsummary)
library(gt)
library(mice)

title: Setup
text:
Cohort constants
These implement section 4 of the analysis plan. dialysis_settings_kept keeps in-center dialysis only, which excludes home dialysis as the paper says. The original code did the same by keeping DIALSET codes 1 and 2, but the coding has changed since: in the current USRDS coding, code 1 is home, so the setting is now named rather than numbered. The eGFR restriction (20 or below) and the outcome (early means 10 or above) also follow the original code, where the paper’s text says “less than 20” and “greater than 10”; the two differ only for patients at exactly 20 or exactly 10.


Click to show/hide R Code
# Cohort (analysis-plan.md section 4): years in which dialysis started
study_years <- 2011:2019
minimum_age <- 18

# Dialysis setting kept: in-center dialysis only, as the paper says (home
# dialysis excluded). The coding of DIALSET has changed. The original code kept
# codes 1 and 2 to exclude home dialysis, which was correct for the earlier
# coding (Appendix C format $MESET_CUR: 1 = hospital inpatient, 2 = dialysis
# facility/center, 3 = home). In the current coding ($MESET, 2024 Researcher's
# Guide) 1 = home and 2 = dialysis facility/center, so the same intent now
# keeps code 2 only. usRds labels the codes, so the setting is named here.
# (Decided by Vagish Hemmige, 27 October 2026.)
dialysis_settings_kept <- "DIALYSIS FACILITY/CENTER"

# eGFR restriction (mL/min/1.73 m2): 20 or below, as in the original code
# (the paper says "less than 20"; decided 27 October 2026)
egfr_maximum <- 20

# Outcome (section 7): early initiation is eGFR of 10 or above, as in the
# original code (the paper says "greater than 10"; decided 27 October 2026)
early_egfr_threshold <- 10

# Sensitivity analysis: eGFR range from the original code (exclusive bounds)
sensitivity_egfr_range <- c(5, 25)

# States outside the 48 contiguous states + DC; territories have no region
noncontiguous_states <- c("ALASKA", "HAWAII")

Exposure constants
Density is facilities per 100,000 HSA residents, cut at the 25th, 50th and 75th percentiles of density among patients in the final cohort, as in the original code. The cut points are computed from the data, never typed in; the published ones (1.36, 1.95 and 2.76) appear only in a comment in define_exposure.R, for comparison.

# Cut points: these percentiles of density among patients in the final cohort

title: Setup
text:
Cause of kidney failure
The six categories are those of the paper’s Table 1. The mapping of every USRDS code to a category is drafted by three cloud models, one each from OpenAI, Anthropic and Google, each provider’s current general-purpose model as of October 2026. Codes on which at least two agree are accepted, and the deciders review the rest. Two models run locally through Ollama (Alibaba’s Qwen and Meta’s Llama) answer too and are reported for comparison, without voting (esrd_classifier_voting lists the voting models). Gemini and Qwen get batches of 25 codes rather than 100, and Llama batches of 5 (see Classifying codes; the mapping was accepted as drafted, decided by Vagish Hemmige, 30 October 2026). The models used, the prompt version and the ellmer version are recorded in the output file.


Click to show/hide R Code
# Primary cause of kidney failure (section 6). The mapping of every $PD96DET code
# is in references/esrd-cause-categories.csv (decision D4, settled 30 October 2026).
esrd_cause_categories <- c(
  "Diabetes",
  "Hypertension and cardiac disease",
  "Glomerulonephritis",
  "Hereditary or polycystic kidney disease",
  "Transplant failure or complications",
  "Other"
)
esrd_cause_mapping_file <- "references/esrd-cause-categories.csv"
# One row: how many codes the models agreed on, and Fleiss' kappa
esrd_cause_agreement_file <- "references/esrd-cause-agreement.csv"
# One row per local model: how complete and valid its answers were, and how
# often it agreed with the accepted category (reported, not used to accept)
esrd_local_model_file <- "references/esrd-cause-local-models.csv"

# Models used by R/classify_esrd_causes.R. Three cloud models, each
# provider's current general-purpose model as of October 2026, as in an
# earlier ensemble by the same team (gpt-5.1, claude-sonnet-4-5,
# gemini-2.5-flash); and two local models run through Ollama on the analyst's
# own computer, which send nothing over the internet: Alibaba's Qwen and
# Meta's Llama, from two further companies (decided by Vagish Hemmige, 28 and
# 29 October 2026). Llama 3.1 replaced IBM's Granite (granite4.2:8b) on 29
# October 2026: on the analyst's laptop Granite returned no answers for 5
# codes in 15 minutes. Qwen answers with its "thinking" turned off: with it
# on, its reasoning filled Ollama's working space before the answer was
# written. (Ollama's medical models are all Google's MedGemma, which would
# overlap with Gemini, or older models built on Llama 2.) Change a name here
# to use another model; the models used are recorded in the output.
#
# Only the three cloud models vote. The local models are run and reported
# for comparison, but do not vote (decided by Vagish Hemmige, 29 October
# 2026): on the analyst's laptop neither produced a complete, valid set of
# answers. Both left codes unanswered, returned text that is not a code (a
# code in quotation marks, "</code>" fragments, web addresses, codes not in
# the list) and gave categories that contradict their own reasons.
esrd_classifier_models <- list(
  openai = "gpt-6.1-terra",
  anthropic = "claude-sonnet-5-5",
  google = "gemini-3.8-flash",
  ollama_qwen = "qwen3.5:9b",
  ollama_llama = "llama3.1:8b"
)
esrd_classifier_voting <- c("openai", "anthropic", "google")
# Codes sent per call. Gemini timed out on batches of 100, and local models
# are slower and handle less text at once, so they get smaller batches. On the
# analyst's laptop, Llama 3.1 answered only 7 of a batch of 25 codes but all of
# a batch of 5 (29 October 2026)
esrd_classifier_batch_sizes <- list(
  openai = 100,
  anthropic = 100,
  google = 25,
  ollama_qwen = 25,
  ollama_llama = 5
)
# A category is accepted when at least this many of the three voting models
# give it: 2 of 3, a majority (decided by Vagish Hemmige, 29 October 2026,
# when the local models stopped voting; the rule had been 3 of 5). Other codes
# go to the deciders.
esrd_classifier_min_agreement <- 2
esrd_classifier_prompt_file <- "prompts/esrd-cause-classification.md"
# Output limit for Claude. ellmer 0.5.0 caps Claude's answers at 4,096 tokens
# unless told otherwise, too few for a batch of 100 codes with reasons; the
# other providers have no default cap in ellmer.
esrd_classifier_claude_max_tokens <- 16000
# Seconds to wait for one answer. ellmer's default, 5 minutes, is too short
# for a local model on a laptop processor; the cloud models answer well within
# either limit.
esrd_classifier_timeout_s <- 30 * 60
# Each provider's checked answers are saved here (gitignored), so a rerun does
# not pay for a provider that already finished
esrd_votes_dir <- file.path(public_data_dir, "esrd-cause-votes")

title: Setup
text:
Model constants
The covariate sets follow the footnotes of the paper’s Table 2, and Model 3’s HSA benchmarks are the three the paper’s Methods name. The logistic models are fit with glmmTMB (Laplace approximation); the models page explains why.


Click to show/hide R Code
# Mixed-effects logistic models (section 8) are fit with glmmTMB, using the
# Laplace approximation. On synthetic data shaped like Model 3, lme4::glmer
# needed rescaled covariates and a higher iteration limit to converge and took
# about 30 times longer, for the same estimates; adaptive quadrature with 7
# points (Stata's default) changed the odds ratios only in the third decimal
# (decided by Vagish Hemmige, 27 October 2026).
imputation_count <- 10
imputation_seed <- 20231020

# Covariates added at each step of Table 2 (section 8), from the Table 2
# footnotes; the HSA benchmarks are the three the Methods name
# Year of hemodialysis initiation, as the paper's Methods say; the original R
# code used the year of the form (decided 27 October 2026)
model_1_covariates <- c("age", "sex", "race", "hispanic", "dialysis_year")
model_2_covariates <- c(model_1_covariates,
                        "heart_failure", "coronary_disease", "diabetes",
                        "cerebrovascular_disease", "alcohol_or_drug", "immobility",
                        "institutionalized", "access_type", "esrd_cause")
model_2_laboratory <- c("albumin", "hemoglobin")
model_3_covariates <- c(model_2_covariates,
                        "insurance", "nephrology_care", "rural_urban",
                        "zip_percent_poverty", "zip_percent_black",
                        "hsa_ambulatory_sensitive_discharges",
                        "hsa_percent_eye_exam", "hsa_percent_hba1c")

6. Density categories
3. USRDS patient data
text: Loads the Medical Evidence and Residence files through usRds and derives the patient-level variables. No patients are removed at this step; every exclusion is a step in the cohort flowchart.

title: 3. USRDS patient data
text:
Loading the Medical Evidence file
usRds finds the file in the folder set by set_USRDS_wd() and applies the USRDS value labels from Appendix C of the Researcher’s Guide (United States Renal Data System 2024), so codes become their documented meanings. That is how the replication found that the coding of DIALSET has changed: code 1 now means home dialysis, where in the coding the original code was written for it meant hospital inpatient. The original code typed the codes and their meanings by hand. The primary cause of kidney failure (PDIS) is kept as the raw code because several codes share a description.


Click to show/hide R Code
# usRds applies the USRDS value labels (Appendix C), so codes become their
# documented meanings (for example DIALSET 1 = "HOME").
medevid_columns <- c(
  "USRDS_ID", "MEFDATE", "DIALDAT", "INC_AGE", "SEX", "RACE", "ETHN",
  "DIALTYP", "DIALSET", "GFR_EPI", "SERCR", "ALBUM", "HEGLB", "WEIGHT", "HEIGHT",
  "ACCESSTYPE", "NEPHCARE", "PDIS", "CDTYPE"
)

# The provider ID column is PROVUSRD_DIAL in the 2024 Researcher's Guide and
# PROVUSRD in older releases; whichever the release has is used.
provider_columns <- c("PROVUSRD_DIAL", "PROVUSRD")

# PDIS is kept as the raw code, because several codes share a description and
# the cause mapping is by code. It is renamed while the labels are applied, so
# usRds does not recognize it, and then renamed back.
medevid_labelled <- load_usrds_file("MEDEVID", factor_labels = FALSE) |>
  select(
    any_of(medevid_columns),
    any_of(provider_columns),
    starts_with("MEDCOV_"),
    starts_with("COMO_")
  ) |>
  rename(PDIS_CODE = PDIS) |>
  apply_usrds_factors(file_key = "MEDEVID") |>
  rename(PDIS = PDIS_CODE) |>
  mutate(PDIS = str_trim(as.character(PDIS)))

title: 3. USRDS patient data
text:
Patient variables
Each form is numbered within its patient, and the first form is flagged. Race is grouped into the paper’s five groups. How the Stata analysis merged the form’s other codes is not recorded, so for this demonstration Middle Eastern counts as White and South Asian as Asian, following the 1997 OMB race standard (Office of Management and Budget 1997), and Other or multiracial counts as White, the largest group. These patients are therefore in the White stratum of the race-stratified models (eTables 1 and 2). The detailed race is kept as race_detailed.
The clinical variables are derived as follows:

Comorbidities are present when any of their form fields is marked yes; blank or unknown counts as not present, as on the form. Diabetes combines four fields (insulin, oral medication, no medication, retinopathy), alcohol or drug dependence two, immobility three (inability to ambulate, needing assistance, inability to transfer) and institutionalized four (any type of institution).
Insurance follows the original code’s order: no insurance, then Medicaid, then Medicare or managed Medicare, then commercial (employer group), then other, including the VA.
Nephrology care before kidney failure is no, some or unknown (NEPHCARE), with unknown kept as its own level.
Early start is an eGFR of 10 or above at initiation. The facility ID is PROVUSRD in older releases and PROVUSRD_DIAL in the 2024 guide.

Functions used: any_yes(), derive_insurance(), derive_nephrology_care(), first_non_missing().


Click to show/hide R Code
medevid_forms <- medevid_labelled |>
  arrange(USRDS_ID, MEFDATE) |>
  mutate(form_order = row_number(), .by = USRDS_ID) |>
  mutate(
    first_form = form_order == 1,
    year = as.integer(year(MEFDATE)),
    dialysis_year = as.integer(year(DIALDAT)),
    age = INC_AGE,
    sex = factor(str_to_title(SEX), levels = c("Male", "Female")),
    race_detailed = as.character(RACE),
    race = case_when(
      RACE == "WHITE" ~ "White",
      RACE == "BLACK" ~ "Black",
      RACE == "ASIAN" ~ "Asian",
      RACE == "AMERICAN INDIAN/ALASKAN NATIVE" ~ "Native American",
      RACE == "PACIFIC ISLANDER" ~ "Pacific Islander",
      # The paper reports five groups. Middle Eastern is counted as White and
      # South Asian as Asian (the OMB 1997 race standard), and Other or
      # multiracial as White, the largest group; how Stata grouped them is
      # not recorded (chosen for this demonstration, 27 October 2026)
      RACE == "MIDEAST" ~ "White",
      RACE == "INDIAN SUBCO" ~ "Asian",
      RACE == "OTHER/MULTI-RACIAL" ~ "White",
      .default = NA_character_
    ),
    race = factor(race, levels = c(
      "White", "Black", "Asian", "Native American", "Pacific Islander"
    )),
    hispanic = case_when(
      ETHN %in% c("HISPANIC-MEXICAN", "HISPANIC OTHER", "HISPANIC NON-SPECIFIED") ~ "Hispanic",
      ETHN == "NON-HISPANIC" ~ "Non-Hispanic",
      .default = NA_character_
    ),
    hispanic = factor(hispanic, levels = c("Non-Hispanic", "Hispanic")),
    egfr = GFR_EPI,
    early_start = as.integer(egfr >= early_egfr_threshold),
    albumin = ALBUM,
    hemoglobin = HEGLB,
    access_type = case_when(
      ACCESSTYPE == "AVF" ~ "Arteriovenous fistula",
      ACCESSTYPE == "GRAFT" ~ "Arteriovenous graft",
      ACCESSTYPE == "CATH" ~ "Catheter",
      ACCESSTYPE == "OTHER" ~ "Other",
      .default = NA_character_
    ),
    access_type = factor(access_type, levels = c(
      "Catheter", "Arteriovenous fistula", "Arteriovenous graft", "Other"
    )),
    nephrology_care = derive_nephrology_care(NEPHCARE),
    insurance = derive_insurance(
      none = MEDCOV_NONE,
      medicaid = MEDCOV_MDCD,
      medicare = MEDCOV_MDCR,
      advantage = MEDCOV_ADVANTAGE,
      group = MEDCOV_GROUP,
      va = MEDCOV_DVA,
      other = MEDCOV_OTHER
    ),
    insurance = factor(insurance, levels = c(
      "Medicare or managed Medicare", "No insurance", "Medicaid",
      "Commercial", "Other (including VA)"
    )),
    heart_failure = as.integer(any_yes(COMO_CHF)),
    coronary_disease = as.integer(any_yes(COMO_ASHD)),
    diabetes = as.integer(any_yes(COMO_DM_INS, COMO_DM_ORAL, COMO_DM_NOMEDS, COMO_DM_RET)),
    cerebrovascular_disease = as.integer(any_yes(COMO_CVATIA)),
    cancer = as.integer(any_yes(COMO_CANC)),
    alcohol_or_drug = as.integer(any_yes(COMO_ALCHO, COMO_DRUG)),
    immobility = as.integer(any_yes(COMO_INAMB, COMO_NEEDASST, COMO_INTRANS)),
    institutionalized = as.integer(any_yes(COMO_INST, COMO_INST_AL, COMO_INST_NURS, COMO_INST_OTH)),
    dialysis_provider = first_non_missing(pick(any_of(provider_columns)))
  )

title: About
text:
This repository
This repository rebuilds the published analysis from a single R Markdown file into scripts run in order by R/main.R, using usRds, flowchart and tidycensus. It accompanies a 2026 abstract on the reproducibility of USRDS research. The USRDS data are restricted and are not in the repository; the code finds them through usRds on the computer of an authorized analyst.
Contributions follow the rules in AGENTS.md; open decisions and known issues are tracked in Issues.

title: About
text:
How this website was created
The site is built with Quarto from the analysis scripts themselves. Each page imports the labelled sections of its script from R/ and shows them with an explanation; the site never runs the analysis, so it is built without the restricted USRDS data.
The repository was set up, and is maintained, with the R Analysis Workflow plugin for AI coding assistants (Claude and ChatGPT), written by Vagish Hemmige. The plugin provides the repository layout, the conventions for the analysis plan and AGENTS.md, the format of these pages, and independent reviews; the architecture document is generated with Posit’s describe-design skill. AI assistants (Claude and ChatGPT) drafted code, documentation and suggestions under the rules in AGENTS.md: they work only with code, documentation and synthetic data, never with USRDS data, and every scientific decision is made by the investigators and recorded in a GitHub issue.
Four documents describe the project. In short: the plan is the scientific intent, the architecture is the workflow as implemented, and AGENTS.md holds the rules for working together.

Analysis plan: what the analysis is meant to do, and why. The question, the study population, the variables, the statistical methods, and the choices that need the investigators’ judgment, with each open choice linked to its decision issue. It is written and decided by the investigators; code implements it and does not redefine it.
Architecture: how the code does it. The scripts, the order they run in, what each needs and produces, and how data flow between them. It describes only what is implemented, so a collaborator can find a step without reading every script.
AGENTS.md: how people and AI assistants work on the project. Rules for restricted data, coding, testing, proposing changes and getting a person’s approval.
Repository blueprint: the layout every project of this kind starts from, which the architecture document then describes as built.

title: About
text:
Pages

Clinical background: why the timing of dialysis and facility density matter.
The original R Markdown file: the October 2023 analysis, formatted, with each code chunk folded.
Differences from the original code: every correction and open decision, with a glossary of USRDS terms.
Setup: packages and every constant.
Functions: tested helper functions.
1. Public area data: ACS, Dartmouth Atlas and RUCA downloads.
2. Cause of kidney failure: the mapping of cause codes, drafted by an ensemble of language models and reviewed by the deciders.
3. USRDS patient data: Medical Evidence and Residence files through usRds.
4. Linking area data: facility counts by date, area data and the exposure.
5. Cohort flowchart: every exclusion as one flowchart step.
6. Density categories: the five exposure categories.
7. Models: Table 2 and sensitivity analyses.
Tables and Figures: building and exporting the outputs.
Published figures and tables: the article’s Figures 1 and 2 and Tables 1 and 2, reproduced unchanged.
Published supplement: the published eTables and eFigures, reproduced unchanged.

This is the analysis file from October 2023 that produced the published cohort and Table 1 (Hemmige et al. 2024). It is kept for comparison: the differences page lists each place where the replication departs from it, and why.

It is shown below as it would read when knitted, with its prose formatted, but nothing in it is run. Each code chunk is folded under a header giving its number, its label and options from the file (some chunks were set to eval=FALSE in 2023 and did not run then either), and its line numbers in the file, so a line cited elsewhere can be found. File_List_txt_clean<-tibble(File_List_txt_raw)%>%

#Define input function for CSV
dialysis_read_csv<-function(x) {
read_csv(x, col_types = cols(Zip = col_character()),
         locale=locale(encoding="latin1"))%>%
    rename_with(toupper)%>%
    rename(TOTSTAS='# OF DIALYSIS STATIONS')%>%
    rename_with(~case_when(
      .=="PROFIT OR NON-PROFIT"~"PROFIT_STATUS",
      .=="PROFIT OR NON-PROFIT?"~"PROFIT_STATUS",
      TRUE~.
    ))%>%
    select(ZIP, TOTSTAS, PROFIT_STATUS)%>%
    mutate(ZIP=case_when(
      str_length(ZIP)==5~ZIP,
      str_length(ZIP)==4~paste0(0,ZIP),
      str_length(ZIP)==3~paste0(0,0,ZIP),
    ))%>%
    group_by(ZIP)%>%
    summarize(TotalDialysisCentersZIP=n(), 
              TotalDialysisStationsZIP=sum(TOTSTAS),
              TotalProfitDialysisCentersZIP=sum(PROFIT_STATUS=="Profit"),
              TotalProfitDialysisStationsZIP=sum(TOTSTAS[PROFIT_STATUS=="Profit"]),
              TotalNonProfitDialysisCentersZIP=sum(PROFIT_STATUS=="Non-Profit"),
              TotNonProfitDialysisStationsZIP=sum(TOTSTAS[PROFIT_STATUS=="Non-Profit"])
              )%>%
    return()
}

#Define input function for TXT
dialysis_read_txt<-function(x) {
  read_delim(x, "\t", escape_double = FALSE, col_types = cols(phyzip = col_character()), trim_ws = TRUE) %>%
    rename_with(toupper)%>%
    rename(ZIP= PHYZIP)%>%
    rename(PROFIT_STATUS=OWNTYPE)%>%
    select(ZIP, TOTSTAS, PROFIT_STATUS)%>%
    mutate(ZIP=case_when(
      str_length(ZIP)==5~ZIP,
      str_length(ZIP)==4~paste0(0,ZIP),
      str_length(ZIP)==3~paste0(0,0,ZIP),
    ))%>%
    group_by(ZIP)%>%
    summarize(TotalDialysisCentersZIP=n(), 
              TotalDialysisStationsZIP=sum(TOTSTAS),
              TotalProfitDialysisCentersZIP=sum(PROFIT_STATUS==1),
              TotalProfitDialysisStationsZIP=sum(TOTSTAS[PROFIT_STATUS==1]),
              TotalNonProfitDialysisCentersZIP=sum(PROFIT_STATUS==2),
              TotNonProfitDialysisStationsZIP=sum(TOTSTAS[PROFIT_STATUS==2])
              )%>%
    return()
}

#Create data list of CSV files
data_csv_clean<-File_List_csv_clean%>%
  mutate(file_contents = map(FileName,~dialysis_read_csv(.)))

#Create data list of TXT files
data_txt_clean<-File_List_txt_clean%>%
  mutate(file_contents = map(FileName,~dialysis_read_txt(.)))

#Combine data
data_combined_clean<-bind_rows(data_csv_clean, data_txt_clean)%>%
  #Create a variable which stores the year
  mutate(Year=str_extract(FileName, "20[0-9][0-9]"))%>%
  #Create temp var which stores time as 4 digit year, 2 digit month, 2 digit day if filename uses this format
  mutate(time=parse_number(FileName))%>%
  mutate(time=ifelse(time>10000,time,NA))%>%
  mutate(time=as.character(time))%>%
  #Create a variable which stores the month
  mutate(Month=ifelse(is.na(time), str_extract(FileName, "_[0-1][0-9]_"), str_sub(time,5,6) ))%>%
  mutate(Month=parse_number(Month))%>%
  #Create a variable which stores the day of month; assume first of the month for more recent years
  mutate(Day=ifelse(is.na(time), 1, str_sub(time,7,8) ))%>%
  #Create a DateStart variable:
  mutate(DateStart=paste0(Year,"-",Month,"-",Day))%>%
  mutate(DateStart=as.Date(DateStart))%>%
  select(-time, -Year, -Month, -Day)%>%
  arrange(DateStart)%>%
  mutate(DateEnd=lead(DateStart)-1)%>%
  filter(!is.na(DateEnd))%>%
  #Expand data set based on duration
  mutate(Duration=DateEnd-DateStart+1)%>%
  mutate(Duration=as.numeric((Duration)))%>%
  uncount(Duration)%>%
  group_by(FileName)%>%
  mutate(N=row_number()-1)%>%
  mutate(DateCurrent=N+DateStart)%>%
  ungroup
  
  
  
#Unnest data
data_combined_clean_unnested<-data_combined_clean%>%
  unnest(cols=file_contents)%>%
  arrange(ZIP, DateCurrent)%>%
  select(-N, -DateStart, -DateEnd, -FileName)
  
#Remove unneeded files
rm(data_combined_clean)
gc()

  select(RACE, ETHN, MEFDATE, SEX, DIALDAT, SERCR, TDATE, WEIGHT, HEIGHT, PROVUSRD, USRDS_ID, INC_AGE, GFR_MDRD, 
         GFR_EPI, DIALSET, DIALTYP, NEPHCARE, NEPHCARERANGE, PDIS, CDTYPE, ALBUM, HEGLB, 
         ACCESSTYPE, AVFMATURING, AVGMATURING, starts_with("MEDCOV"), starts_with("COMO"))%>%
  arrange(USRDS_ID, MEFDATE)%>%
  group_by(USRDS_ID)%>%
  mutate(N=row_number())%>%
  ungroup()%>%
  mutate(Year=year(MEFDATE))%>%
  mutate(RACE=factor(RACE,
         levels=c("1","11","2","3","4","41","5","6","9"),

#Define a Hispanic ethnicity variable
    mutate(HISPANIC=factor(ETHN,

  select(-ETHN)%>%

#Create labelled factor variable for access type
  mutate(ACCESSTYPE=ifelse(ACCESSTYPE==5, NA, ACCESSTYPE))%>%
  mutate(
    ACCESSTYPE=factor(ACCESSTYPE,
         levels=c("1","2","3", "4"),

  )%>%
#Create labelled factor variables for presence of fistula/graft at time of HD initiation
  mutate(AVFMATURING=ifelse(AVFMATURING==9, NA, AVFMATURING))%>%
  mutate(

  mutate(AVGMATURING=ifelse(AVGMATURING==9, NA, AVGMATURING))%>%

    AVGMATURING=factor(AVGMATURING,

  )%>%
  
  #Create variable based on insurance status
  mutate(INSURANCESTATUS=case_when(
    MEDCOV_NONE=="Y"~"No insurance",
    MEDCOV_MDCD=="Y"~"Medicaid/Dual eligible/Managed Medicaid",
    MEDCOV_MDCR=="Y"~"Medicare/managed Medicare",
    MEDCOV_ADVANTAGE=="Y"~"Medicare/managed Medicare",
    MEDCOV_GROUP=="Y"~"Commercial",
    MEDCOV_DVA=="Y"~"Other",

#Convert a number of factor variables
  mutate(SEX=as.factor(SEX))%>%
  mutate(DIALSET=as.factor(DIALSET))%>%
  mutate(DIALTYP=as.factor(DIALTYP))%>%
  mutate(CDTYPE=as.factor(CDTYPE))%>%
  mutate(PROVUSRD=as.factor(PROVUSRD))%>%
  mutate(INSURANCESTATUS=as.factor(INSURANCESTATUS))%>%
  mutate(across(.cols = starts_with("MEDCOV"),
                .fns = factor
                ))%>%
  mutate(across(.cols = starts_with("COMO_"),

    select(starts_with("zipcode"), hsanum)%>%
    pivot_longer(

      names_to = "year",

    mutate(year=as.numeric(year))%>%
    mutate(year=2000+year)%>%
    mutate(zipcode=as.character(zipcode))%>%
    mutate(zipcode=case_when(
      nchar(zipcode)==3~paste0("00",zipcode),
      nchar(zipcode)==4~paste0("0",zipcode),
      nchar(zipcode)==5~zipcode))%>%
    
    
    return
  
}

title: 4. Linking area data
text: For each patient’s first Medical Evidence form, this script adds what is known about the place they lived: the number of dialysis facilities in their ZIP code and HSA on the day dialysis started, census (ACS) data for the ZIP code, the HSA’s population and Dartmouth Atlas benchmarks, whether the area is rural or urban, and the cause of kidney failure. It then calculates the study’s exposure, dialysis facilities per 100,000 HSA residents. No patients are removed at this step; those with missing area data are excluded later, as steps in the cohort flowchart.

title: 4. Linking area data
text:
Facility density
Facilities per 100,000 HSA residents, plus the availability flags the flowchart filters on. A patient has an HSA only if the HSA’s density is a finite number: an HSA whose population is zero would give an infinite density, so it counts as having no HSA.


Click to show/hide R Code
# Facilities per 100,000 HSA residents on the date of dialysis start.
linked_forms <- linked_forms |>
  mutate(
    hsa_center_density = centers_area / hsa_population * density_per_population,
    hsa_station_density = stations_area / hsa_population * density_per_population,
    has_zcta = !is.na(zcta),
    has_acs = !is.na(zip_population),
    has_facility_snapshot = !is.na(facility_snapshot_date),
    has_hsa = !is.na(hsanum) & !is.na(hsa_center_density) & is.finite(hsa_center_density),
    has_complete_acs = if_all(all_of(acs_variables$name), \(x) !is.na(x)),
    has_ruca = !is.na(ruca1) & ruca1 != ruca_not_coded
  ) |>
  set_variable_labels(
    centers_zip = "Dialysis facilities in the ZIP code on the date of dialysis start",
    stations_zip = "Dialysis stations in the ZIP code on the date of dialysis start",
    centers_area = "Dialysis facilities in the HSA on the date of dialysis start",
    stations_area = "Dialysis stations in the HSA on the date of dialysis start",
    profit_centers_area = "For-profit dialysis facilities in the HSA on the date of dialysis start",
    nonprofit_centers_area = "Non-profit dialysis facilities in the HSA on the date of dialysis start",
    zcta = "ZCTA of the residential ZIP code (UDS Mapper crosswalk, dialysis start year)",
    hsanum = "Dartmouth Atlas HSA (crosswalk for the dialysis start year)",
    hsa_population = "HSA population (sum of ACS ZCTA populations, dialysis start year)",
    hsa_center_density = "HSA dialysis facilities per 100,000 residents",
    hsa_station_density = "HSA dialysis stations per 100,000 residents",
    rural_urban = "Rural-urban type (primary RUCA code, 2010)",
    esrd_cause = "Presumed cause of kidney failure"
  )

rm(first_forms, facility_crosswalk, esrd_cause_mapping, unreviewed_codes)

Analytical scripts

R/main.R sources definitive scripts in dependency order.
Typical workflow: setup → cohort construction → processing → modeling → outputs.
Study-specific scripts may be grouped into subdirectories by analytical stage.
R/tables.R and R/figures.R may generate outputs directly or orchestrate specialized scripts.

Documentation

Document definitive analytical scripts with explanatory Quarto pages; exploratory scripts need not have pages.
Use Cryptococcus-cost-analysis as an example for Quarto supporting files, chunk imports, callouts, and formatting—not scientific methods.
Quarto source and rendered output locations may vary by project.

Outputs and version control

Track approved, nonrestricted outputs when useful for publication; otherwise retain them locally and exclude them from Git.
.gitignore: Exclude restricted data, credentials, caches, temporary files, and generated outputs unless intentionally tracked (e.g., .Rproj.user/, .Rhistory, .RData, .httr-oauth, .quarto/, cache/, figures/, tables/, *.quarto_ipynb); verify exclusions cover actual output paths without hiding necessary source or reference files.

title: Tables
text: Builds Table 1 and the regression tables, and exports them to the gitignored tables/ folder.

title: Tables
text:
Table 1
Patient and HSA characteristics by density category: the same 25 characteristics as the paper’s Table 1, with means (SD), counts (%), classical one-way ANOVA for continuous characteristics and chi-squared tests for categorical ones. The paper says one-way ANOVA, so R’s oneway.test() is run with var.equal = TRUE; its default is Welch’s version, which does not assume equal variances across categories (decided by Vagish Hemmige, 28 October 2026). With this many patients the two give almost the same P values. The paper also lists the Kruskal-Wallis test without saying which characteristics it was used for. The layout (sections, missing counts and column headers) is gtsummary’s default, not the paper’s.


Click to show/hide R Code
table_1_variables <- c(
  "age", "sex", "race", "hispanic",
  "heart_failure", "coronary_disease", "diabetes", "cerebrovascular_disease",
  "cancer", "immobility", "alcohol_or_drug",
  "nephrology_care", "albumin", "hemoglobin", "access_type", "insurance",
  "esrd_cause", "zip_percent_black", "zip_percent_poverty",
  "hsa_ambulatory_sensitive_discharges", "hsa_percent_mammogram",
  "hsa_percent_hba1c", "hsa_percent_eye_exam", "profit_centers_area", "rural_urban"
)

table_1 <- cohort |>
  select(density_category, all_of(table_1_variables)) |>
  tbl_summary(
    by = density_category,
    statistic = list(all_continuous() ~ "{mean} ({sd})"),
    digits = list(all_continuous() ~ 1),
    missing = "ifany"
  ) |>
  # Classical one-way ANOVA, as the paper says (var.equal = TRUE; the default
  # of oneway.test() is Welch's test). Decided by Vagish Hemmige, 28 October 2026.
  add_p(
    test = list(all_continuous() ~ "oneway.test", all_categorical() ~ "chisq.test"),
    test.args = all_continuous() ~ list(var.equal = TRUE)
  ) |>
  modify_spanning_header(all_stat_cols() ~ "**HSA facility density per 100,000 population**")

# Download a file into data-raw/ unless it is already there; return its path.
download_once <- function(url, file_name) {
  path <- file.path(public_data_dir, file_name)
  if (!file.exists(path)) {
    download.file(url, path, mode = "wb", quiet = TRUE)
  }
  path
}

HSA population
The denominator of the exposure: the population of the ZCTAs of the ZIP codes in each HSA that year. Because several ZIP codes can share a ZCTA, each ZCTA is counted once per HSA (hsa_population_from_zcta()); summing over ZIP codes would count a shared ZCTA’s population several times.

  zcta_crosswalk,

text:
HSA benchmarks
Primary care measures (2015) and hospital resources (2012). These are the published spreadsheets the original analysis’s Stata files were very likely made from; the code finds each measure’s column by pattern and sets suppression codes to missing.
Functions used: clean_dartmouth_codes(), select_by_pattern(), read_header_table().


Click to show/hide R Code
# HSA primary care measures (2015) and hospital resources (2012). The measure
# columns are found by the patterns in setup.R; -88888 and -99999 become NA.
read_dartmouth_hsa <- function(path, patterns) {
  table <- read_header_table(path, header_pattern = "^HSA")
  id_column <- select_by_pattern(table, c(hsanum = "^hsa[ _.]?(num|id|code)?$"), basename(path))
  measure_columns <- select_by_pattern(table, patterns, basename(path))

  table |>
    select(all_of(id_column), all_of(measure_columns)) |>
    mutate(
      hsanum = as.integer(hsanum),
      across(-hsanum, \(x) clean_dartmouth_codes(x, dartmouth_missing_codes))
    ) |>
    filter(!is.na(hsanum))
}

hsa_benchmarks <- full_join(
  read_dartmouth_hsa(primary_care_file, dartmouth_primary_care_measures),
  read_dartmouth_hsa(capacity_file, dartmouth_capacity_measures),
  by = "hsanum",
  relationship = "one-to-one"
)

title: Dialysis facility density and early dialysis initiation: a replication
text: Hemmige and colleagues studied 844,466 adults who started in-center hemodialysis in the United States from 2011 to 2019, using the US Renal Data System (USRDS) (Hemmige et al. 2024). Patients living in the Hospital Service Areas (HSAs, which the paper calls health service areas) with the most dialysis facilities per resident had higher odds of starting dialysis at an estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) above 10 mL/min/1.73 m²: an odds ratio of 1.06 (95% CI 1.02 to 1.10) compared with HSAs with no facility. The clinical background page explains why that matters.

title: Dialysis facility density and early dialysis initiation: a replication
text:
What this site does
This repository reproduces the paper’s analysis from public code. The original analysis was a single R Markdown file of more than 3,000 lines (shown here, with local file locations removed). It is rebuilt with packages that do the repetitive work:

usRds (Hemmige 2026) loads and labels the USRDS files, and attaches CMS dialysis facility counts to each patient by the date dialysis started.
flowchart (Satorra et al. 2026) applies every exclusion and counts it at the same time, so the cohort diagram is the cohort.
tidycensus (Walker and Herman, n.d.) downloads the American Community Survey, and every other area-level file is downloaded from its publisher.

Rebuilding the analysis this way turned up several errors in the original code. They are corrected here, and each one is listed, with what it can change, on the differences page. Where the original code and the paper disagree, the choice is left to the investigators.

title: Dialysis facility density and early dialysis initiation: a replication
text:
Methods
The authoritative specification is analysis-plan.md. In brief: incident adults on in-center hemodialysis with an eGFR of 20 or below; exposure, HSA dialysis facilities per 100,000 residents in five categories; outcome, eGFR of 10 or above at initiation; mixed-effects logistic models with a random intercept for HSA, progressively adjusted for patient, clinical, area and HSA characteristics. Reporting follows STROBE (Elm et al. 2007), as in the paper, and RECORD (Benchimol et al. 2015), added for the replication.

title: Dialysis facility density and early dialysis initiation: a replication
text:
Status
The code is complete and tested on synthetic data. It has not yet been run on the USRDS data, so this site shows code and methods only; no results from USRDS data are published here. Open decisions are listed on the differences page and tracked as GitHub issues.
The replication also serves as a demonstration of how an analysis like this can be rebuilt with current tools. Where neither the paper nor the original code settles a choice, a few were made for the demonstration rather than by a full scientific review: the rule accepting a cause-of-kidney-failure code when two of three language models agree, and the grouping of race into the paper’s five groups. They affect the Table 1 cause and race rows, the covariates of Models 1 to 3, and the race-stratified eTables. Each is marked “chosen for this demonstration” where it is described.

title: Published supplement
text:
Notes on the published tables
These look like typographical errors in the published supplement. They are kept above as printed and are listed here so that the replication’s tables can be compared with what the authors intended.

The fourth density category is printed as “4(1.05-2.76)”; the main text and Table 1 define it as >1.95 to 2.76.
eTable 1: the Black-only analysis gives n=146,386 in its heading and N=236,947 in the table; the White-only analysis, described as “without Albumin and Hemoglobin”, gives n=355,564 and N=558,364.
eTable 2: the model without albumin and hemoglobin gives n=844,467; the main text gives 844,466. The Black-only n is 235,947 here and 236,947 in eTable 1. One interval is printed “1.01(.00-1.01)”.
eTable 3: the reference categories are printed as “1”; for a linear model of eGFR the reference difference is 0. N=866,467 in the first panel. The category 3 Model 1 estimate is printed “0.4(-0.02-0.12)”, outside its own interval; the category 5 Model 2 interval is printed “(0.29-0.19)”. The category 2 Model 2 estimate, -0.08(-0.15-+0.006), has P=0.7.

title: 7. Models
text: Fits the models behind Table 2 and eTables 1 to 3. The paper’s models were fit in Stata; these are rebuilt from its text and table footnotes.

title: 7. Models
text:
Model data
Year enters as a factor and the reference category is zero facilities, as in the paper.
Functions used: mixed_formula().


Click to show/hide R Code
model_data <- cohort |>
  mutate(
    dialysis_year = factor(dialysis_year),
    density_category = relevel(density_category, ref = levels(density_category)[1])
  )

# Mixed-effects logistic regression with a random intercept for HSA.
# Difference from the paper: the paper fit these models in Stata 15, whose
# default is adaptive Gauss-Hermite quadrature with 7 points; here glmmTMB
# uses the Laplace approximation (1 point). On synthetic data the two gave the
# same odds ratios to two decimals, because each HSA has many patients, and
# glmmTMB converged without rescaling and about 30 times faster than
# lme4::glmer (decided by Vagish Hemmige, 27 October 2026).
fit_logistic <- function(data, exposure, covariates) {
  glmmTMB(
    mixed_formula("early_start", exposure, covariates),
    data = data,
    family = binomial
  )
}

title: 7. Models
text:
Every published model
The paper’s models were fit in Stata, and several of them were never in the original R code: the R file had exploratory models only. The replication fits every model the paper and its supplement report, as they are presented (decided by Vagish Hemmige, 27 October 2026):
