Each block has Models 1 to 3. The models are listed in one table, one row per published column, so nothing reported is missed and a model that appears in two blocks (Model 1 in both blocks of Table 2) is fit once. Model 1 never includes albumin or hemoglobin and uses all patients of its group, as in Table 2, where it is identical in both blocks. Within a race group, race is not a covariate. The eTable 1 headings disagree on whether albumin and hemoglobin are included (see the supplement); both of its sample sizes match the complete-case models, so they are included.


Click to show/hide R Code
# Every model the paper and its supplement report, one row per column of a
# published table: the table, the block of rows it sits in, the outcome
# (early start, or eGFR for eTable 3), the exposure (density category, or
# continuous density for eTable 2), the patients, whether Models 2 and 3
# include albumin and hemoglobin, and whether those two are multiply imputed.
# Model 1 never includes albumin or hemoglobin and is fit on all patients of
# its group, as in Table 2, where it is the same in both blocks.
published_rows <- function(table, block, outcome, exposure, patients, labs,
                           imputed = FALSE) {
  tibble(
    table, block, outcome, exposure, patients, labs, imputed,
    model = c("Model 1", "Model 2", "Model 3")
  )
}

published_models <- bind_rows(
  published_rows("Table 2", "With albumin and hemoglobin",
                 "early_start", "density_category", "All", labs = TRUE),
  published_rows("Table 2", "Without albumin and hemoglobin",
                 "early_start", "density_category", "All", labs = FALSE),
  published_rows("Table 2", "Without HSAs with 0 facilities",
                 "early_start", "density_category", "Without 0-facility HSAs", labs = FALSE),
  published_rows("eTable 1", "Black individuals",
                 "early_start", "density_category", "Black", labs = TRUE),
  published_rows("eTable 1", "White individuals",
                 "early_start", "density_category", "White", labs = TRUE),
  published_rows("eTable 2", "With albumin and hemoglobin",
                 "early_start", "hsa_center_density", "All", labs = TRUE),
  published_rows("eTable 2", "Without albumin and hemoglobin",
                 "early_start", "hsa_center_density", "All", labs = FALSE),
  published_rows("eTable 2", "Albumin and hemoglobin multiply imputed",
                 "early_start", "hsa_center_density", "All", labs = TRUE, imputed = TRUE),
  published_rows("eTable 2", "Black individuals, without albumin and hemoglobin",
                 "early_start", "hsa_center_density", "Black", labs = FALSE),
  published_rows("eTable 2", "White individuals, without albumin and hemoglobin",
                 "early_start", "hsa_center_density", "White", labs = FALSE),
  published_rows("eTable 3", "With albumin and hemoglobin",
                 "egfr", "density_category", "All", labs = TRUE),
  published_rows("eTable 3", "Without HSAs with 0 facilities, with albumin and hemoglobin",
                 "egfr", "density_category", "Without 0-facility HSAs", labs = TRUE)
)

# The covariates of each model; race is left out within a race group
model_covariates <- function(model, labs, patients) {
  covariates <- switch(
    model,
    "Model 1" = model_1_covariates,
    "Model 2" = model_2_covariates,
    "Model 3" = model_3_covariates
  )

  if (labs && model != "Model 1") {
    covariates <- c(covariates, model_2_laboratory)
  }
  if (patients %in% c("White", "Black")) {
    covariates <- setdiff(covariates, "race")
  }
  covariates
}

published_models <- published_models |>
  mutate(covariates = pmap(list(model, labs, patients), model_covariates))

# The patients of each group
patient_groups <- list(
  "All" = model_data,
  "White" = filter(model_data, race == "White"),
  "Black" = filter(model_data, race == "Black"),
  "Without 0-facility HSAs" = model_data |>
    filter(density_category != levels(density_category)[1]) |>
    mutate(density_category = droplevels(density_category))
)

title: 7. Models
text:
Models
Mixed-effects models with a random intercept for HSA, progressively adjusted, fit with glmmTMB (Brooks et al. 2017): logistic for early start, linear for eGFR. With albumin and hemoglobin, patients missing either value drop out of Models 2 and 3, as in the paper’s complete-case models. The covariates follow the paper’s Table 2 footnotes; the “HSA quality benchmarks” in Model 3 are taken to be the three the paper’s Methods give as examples (“such as”: HbA1c testing and eye examinations among enrollees with diabetes, and ambulatory-sensitive discharges).

Choosing the model-fitting package
The paper fit its models in Stata 15 and calls them mixed-effects logit models; it does not name the command. If they were fit with melogit, Stata’s default is adaptive Gauss-Hermite quadrature with 7 points (StataCorp, n.d.).
A mixed model’s likelihood has to be computed by approximation, because each HSA’s random effect is averaged over. The Laplace approximation does this with one point per HSA; adaptive quadrature uses several (here 7), which is more exact but slower. When each HSA has many patients, as here, the two give practically the same answer. In R there are several ways to fit the same model. On synthetic data shaped like Model 3 (4,000 patients, 60 HSAs, about 40 covariate terms), they compared as follows:









Fit
Time
Convergence warnings
Odds ratio, highest vs zero density




lme4::glmer (Bates et al. 2015), default settings
117 s
4
10.08 (not converged)


lme4::glmer, rescaled covariates, higher iteration limit
111 s
0
10.62


lme4::glmer, 7-point quadrature (Stata’s default)
119 s
0
10.63


glmmTMB (Brooks et al. 2017)
4 s
0
10.63



The numbers are synthetic; only the comparison matters. glmmTMB gave the same estimates as a fully converged glmer in about a thirtieth of the time, without rescaling, and quadrature with 7 points rather than the Laplace approximation changed the odds ratios only in the third decimal, because each HSA has many patients. The analysis therefore uses glmmTMB (decided by Vagish Hemmige, 27 October 2026). Three other options were considered:

GLMMadaptive fits the model with adaptive quadrature and any number of points, closest to Stata’s method. It was not timed here.
MixedModels.jl (Alday and Bates, n.d.), a Julia package by Douglas Bates, the original author of lme4, and Phillip Alday, is designed for very large models and can be called from R with the jlme package (Choe 2024). It needs a Julia installation, and jlme is a young, single-maintainer package with little recent activity, so it was not used.
Stata itself, called from R. The RStata package (Braglia 2025) runs Stata commands or a do-file from R and passes a data frame in and out, for example stata("melogit early_start i.density_category ... || hsanum:", data.in = model_data); Stata 17 and later also offer pystata, Stata’s own interface, which R can reach through reticulate. This would keep the paper’s estimation method, if the paper used melogit with its default 7-point adaptive quadrature, but it needs a Stata licence, so it is not part of the public code. Neither Stata nor MixedModels.jl was timed here, so how their speed compares with each other or with glmmTMB on these data is not known.

title: 7. Models
text:
Multiple imputation
The paper reports “a multiple imputation technique with chained predictive analytics (10 imputations)” for albumin and hemoglobin (eTable 2), done in Stata, read here as chained equations; it gives no other detail, and the original R code has none. Here only albumin and hemoglobin are imputed, by predictive mean matching (the mice default for numeric variables (Buuren and Groothuis-Oudshoorn 2011)), from the outcome, the density category and the Model 3 covariates. HSA is not a predictor (about 3,400 levels), and continuous density is not used as a predictor because it duplicates the density category. This imputation model was confirmed by Vagish Hemmige on 28 October 2026 (decision D7).


Click to show/hide R Code
# Multiple imputation of albumin and hemoglobin by chained equations, as the
# paper describes (10 imputations), used for the eTable 2 block that reports
# it. Only albumin and hemoglobin are imputed, by predictive mean matching,
# from the outcome, the density category and the Model 3 covariates. HSA is
# not a predictor (3,400 levels), and continuous density is carried along but
# not used as a predictor, because it duplicates the density category.
imputation_vars <- c(
  "early_start", "density_category", "hsa_center_density", "hsanum",
  model_3_covariates, model_2_laboratory
)
imputation_data <- select(model_data, all_of(imputation_vars))

imputation_method <- make.method(imputation_data)
imputation_method[!names(imputation_method) %in% model_2_laboratory] <- ""

imputation_predictors <- make.predictorMatrix(imputation_data)
imputation_predictors[, c("hsanum", "hsa_center_density")] <- 0

imputed_sets <- mice(
  imputation_data,
  m = imputation_count,
  method = imputation_method,
  predictorMatrix = imputation_predictors,
  seed = imputation_seed,
  printFlag = FALSE
)

title: 7. Models
text:
Fitting
Each distinct model is fit once and its density terms extracted: odds ratios for the logistic models, differences in eGFR for eTable 3, each with a 95% Wald confidence interval. Imputed models are fit on each completed data set and pooled by Rubin’s rules, whose intervals combine the variation within and between the imputed data sets.
Functions used: density_effects(), mixed_formula().


Click to show/hide R Code
# One fit per distinct model; a model that appears in two blocks (Model 1 in
# both blocks of Table 2, for example) is fit once. Logistic models report
# odds ratios; the linear models of eTable 3 report differences in eGFR.
fit_published_model <- function(outcome, exposure, patients, imputed, covariates) {
  # `imputed` (TRUE or FALSE) says whether to use the imputed data sets,
  # imputed_sets
  model_family <- if (outcome == "early_start") binomial() else gaussian()
  formula <- mixed_formula(outcome, exposure, covariates)
  term_pattern <- str_glue("^{exposure}")
  logistic <- outcome == "early_start"

  if (!imputed) {
    fit <- glmmTMB(formula, data = patient_groups[[patients]], family = model_family)
    return(density_effects(fit, term_pattern, exponentiate = logistic))
  }

  # Each completed data set is fitted explicitly and the fits are pooled by
  # Rubin's rules; with(imputed_sets, ...) would not find the variables of a
  # formula built by mixed_formula()
  imputed_sets |>
    mice::complete(action = "all") |>
    map(\(completed) glmmTMB(formula, data = completed, family = model_family)) |>
    as.mira() |>
    pool() |>
    summary(conf.int = TRUE, exponentiate = logistic) |>
    as_tibble() |>
    filter(str_detect(term, term_pattern)) |>
    transmute(
      model = NA_character_,
      term = as.character(term),
      estimate,
      conf_low = `2.5 %`,
      conf_high = `97.5 %`,
      p_value = p.value,
      n = nrow(imputation_data)
    )
}

published_models <- published_models |>
  mutate(fit_key = map_chr(
    transpose(pick(outcome, exposure, patients, imputed, covariates)),
    rlang::hash
  ))

published_fits <- published_models |>
  distinct(fit_key, .keep_all = TRUE) |>
  mutate(result = pmap(
    list(outcome, exposure, patients, imputed, covariates),
    fit_published_model
  )) |>
  select(fit_key, result)

published_estimates <- published_models |>
  left_join(published_fits, by = "fit_key", relationship = "many-to-one") |>
  select(table, block, model, outcome, exposure, result) |>
  unnest(result, names_sep = "_") |>
  select(
    table, block, model, outcome, exposure,
    term = result_term,
    estimate = result_estimate,
    conf_low = result_conf_low,
    conf_high = result_conf_high,
    p_value = result_p_value,
    n = result_n
  )



One model written out
The code above builds every model from the list rather than writing each one out, so no single model appears in it. As an example, this is what it fits for Table 2, Model 3, with albumin and hemoglobin, the paper’s fully adjusted model. Each row of the list becomes a call like this one; the other models drop or add covariates, change the patients, or swap the outcome or exposure.
# Table 2, block "With albumin and hemoglobin", Model 3:
# outcome early_start, exposure density_category, patients "All", labs TRUE
fit <- glmmTMB(
  early_start ~ density_category +
    # Model 1: demographics and year (model_1_covariates)
    age + sex + race + hispanic + dialysis_year +
    # Model 2 adds comorbidities, access and cause (model_2_covariates)
    heart_failure + coronary_disease + diabetes + cerebrovascular_disease +
    alcohol_or_drug + immobility + institutionalized + access_type + esrd_cause +
    # Model 3 adds insurance, nephrology care and area measures (model_3_covariates)
    insurance + nephrology_care + rural_urban + zip_percent_poverty +
    zip_percent_black + hsa_ambulatory_sensitive_discharges +
    hsa_percent_eye_exam + hsa_percent_hba1c +
    # labs = TRUE adds the laboratory values (model_2_laboratory)
    albumin + hemoglobin +
    # random intercept for HSA
    (1 | hsanum),
  data = patient_groups[["All"]],   # model_data: the whole cohort
  family = binomial
)

# The rows reported: odds ratios for the four density categories against
# HSAs with no facility, with 95% CIs, p values and the patients used
density_effects(fit, "^density_category", exponentiate = TRUE)
In the code, model_covariates("Model 3", labs = TRUE, patients = "All") returns these 24 covariates, and mixed_formula() turns them into the formula. A test (tests/test-model-example.R) checks that the formula on this page is the one the code builds, so the example cannot drift from the code.

title: 7. Models
text:
Variance decomposition
How much of the variation in eGFR at initiation lies between HSAs, and between facilities within HSAs, from two null linear mixed models fit by lme4::lmer with its default, restricted maximum likelihood (REML). The nested model cannot use patients with no dialysis facility ID, so both models are fit on the patients who have one; otherwise the two shares would come from different patients (decided by Vagish Hemmige, 28 October 2026).
Functions used: variance_shares().


Click to show/hide R Code
# Share of the variance of eGFR at the HSA and facility levels (null models).
# Both models use the same patients, those with a dialysis facility ID, so the
# shares are comparable (decided by Vagish Hemmige, 28 October 2026).
variance_data <- filter(model_data, !is.na(dialysis_provider))

hsa_variance <- lmer(egfr ~ 1 + (1 | hsanum), data = variance_data) |>
  variance_shares() |>
  mutate(model = "HSA")

facility_variance <- lmer(
  egfr ~ 1 + (1 | hsanum / dialysis_provider),
  data = variance_data
) |>
  variance_shares() |>
  mutate(model = "HSA and facility (nested)")

variance_decomposition <- bind_rows(hsa_variance, facility_variance)

title: 7. Models
text:
eGFR range
A sensitivity analysis from the original R code that is not in the paper: Model 3 among patients with eGFR above 5 and below 25. Because the cohort already has eGFR of 20 or below, it in effect excludes patients with eGFR of 5 or below, and it is labelled that way.
Functions used: density_odds_ratios().


Click to show/hide R Code
# From the original R code, not in the paper: Model 3 among patients with eGFR
# between 5 and 25. The cohort already has eGFR of 20 or below, so in effect
# this excludes patients with eGFR of 5 or below.
egfr_range_estimates <- model_data |>
  filter(egfr > sensitivity_egfr_range[1], egfr < sensitivity_egfr_range[2]) |>
  fit_logistic("density_category", model_3_covariates) |>
  density_odds_ratios(model_name = "Model 3 (without albumin, Hb) - excluding eGFR of 5 or below")

Estimates are saved in the gitignored models/ folder with the usRds version, so tables can be rebuilt without refitting.

Project documentsAGENTS.md Code

The project
This repository replicates a published cross-sectional study of USRDS incident hemodialysis patients, which found that higher dialysis facility density in a patient’s Hospital Service Area (HSA; the paper calls it a health service area) was associated with starting hemodialysis at a higher eGFR (Hemmige et al., JAMA Netw Open 2024, doi:10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2023.50009). The original analysis was one R Markdown file of more than 3,000 lines (kept, with local paths removed, in original/). This version rebuilds it with usRds and flowchart, corrects errors found along the way, and documents each difference. Code and methods are published as a Quarto website.

analysis-plan.md is the source of truth for design. Code implements the plan; it does not redefine it. If code needs to depart from the plan, open a decision issue, or comment on the existing one, for the deciders. Once a decider has settled it (in the issue, or relayed there in their exact words), the plan change and the code can go in the same pull request, which closes the issue.
Deciders. Scientific decisions are made by Vagish Hemmige and Ladan Golestaneh, in any area. Anyone may open or contribute to a decision issue; only a decider settles it (see “Working with agents”).
Replication rule. The original code is evidence of what was done, not the specification. When it disagrees with the paper or contains an error, do not silently copy it or silently fix it: the plan’s section 12 and the site’s “Differences from the original code” page record every difference, and choices between the paper and the code go to a decision issue.
This is an analysis project, not an R package. Do not add DESCRIPTION, NAMESPACE, roxygen, or pkgdown infrastructure, or apply CRAN conventions.
Default branch: main, protected. Changes reach it only through pull requests.

Data sources
Each source this project uses is listed below with the package that accesses it. Code that touches a source goes through its package. Do not write project-specific loading, cleaning, or definition code for something the package already does.

To allow more for a source, a person changes its row through a pull request, naming the agreement and section that permit it, the approved AI service, and exactly what agents may do. Agents never propose or make this change themselves, and nothing in personal instructions can grant it.
For every package:

Read its documentation before writing code for a source, including known issues. Behavior that sets the cohort, an exposure, an outcome, or a denominator is checked in the documentation, not assumed from a function’s name.

For packages this team maintains (usRds):

Facts about the source belong in the package’s documentation, not in this file. If the package lacks something this project needs to know, add it there or open an issue there.
Problems belong in the package. If a function is wrong or does not quite do what the plan needs, open an issue in its repository. Fix it in the package (preferred when generally useful) or wrap it here with a code comment linking the issue, and remove the wrapper once the issue is fixed.
Pending usRds work. The facility functions (dialysis_facility_snapshots, add_dialysis_facility_counts(), summarize_dialysis_facilities()) are being reviewed in the usRds project. Until they are released, this repository needs the usRds version that contains them; record the version or commit used for every result.

For external packages:

Work around problems here. Wrap the function in R/functions.R with a comment explaining the problem and linking any upstream issue. Reporting a bug upstream is an external communication; the person directing the work decides whether to file it.
Facts about the source that this project relies on (definitions, release quirks, suppression rules) go in references/ with a citation to the provider’s documentation, or in the plan when they shape a decision.

For a source with no package: one loading script records the download URL, the release or access date, and any processing. Verify its variables against the provider’s documentation for that release.

Dartmouth Atlas files code small values as -88888 and suppressed values as -99999; these are set to missing, never used as numbers.
ACS subject-table (S0601) variable codes can change between years; R/download_public_data.R checks each year’s labels before use.

Exploration and definitive analysis
Exploration is welcome on branches or forks. Experimental scripts need not be sourced from R/main.R or have Quarto pages, and their findings are labelled preliminary. A script becomes part of the definitive analysis when it is sourced from R/main.R; from then on every rule below applies to it.
R/classify_esrd_causes.R has its place in main.R, after the public data, but its line there is commented out: it is run once, by hand, by an authorized person, because it calls paid APIs; its reviewed output in references/ is what the analysis reads. It has a Quarto page because the mapping is part of the definitive analysis.

R scripts

Running the analysis. Run R/main.R from the project root. It sources the other scripts in dependency order; ARCHITECTURE.md describes what each does.
One job per script. When you add a definitive script, source it from main.R at the right point and update ARCHITECTURE.md in the same pull request.
Header comment. Each script begins with what it does, which objects it needs from earlier scripts, and what it produces.
Constants, libraries, and code lists live in R/setup.R. Other scripts do not call library(), re-source setup.R, or hard-code values. Any number a reader might want to change (a window, a year, a threshold, a ratio) is a named constant there.
Helper functions go in R/functions.R. A function takes its inputs as arguments and does not read global objects.
No side effects outside the project. No setwd(), absolute paths, or writes outside the project. USRDS data are located only through usRds (the USRDS_WD environment variable set by set_USRDS_wd()). Public downloads are cached in the ignored data-raw/ folder.
No results in the repository. No script (exploratory or definitive) or comment, commit message, issue, pull-request text or review report contains results, counts or data values from USRDS data unless they are cleared for release. Check before every commit and post, since a public repository publishes everything pushed to it, on any branch. Numbers quoted from the published paper are public and may be cited.

Chunk labels
Scripts are divided into labelled sections so Quarto pages can show the code without copying it:
## ---- <step-name>

Every logical step has a label. A label covers the code from its line to the next label.
Labels are kebab-case, describe the step, and are unique across all scripts; a duplicate silently picks up the wrong code.
Search the .qmd files before renaming or deleting a label.
Labels are comments and never change what the code does.

Variable labels
Label analysis variables with human-readable descriptions. USRDS variables get their labels from load_usrds_file(var_labels = TRUE); derived variables are labelled where they are created with labelled::set_variable_labels(), with units and the year or date they refer to.

Quarto website
The site documents the code. It does not run the analysis.

_quarto.yml and index.qmd sit at the root; quarto/ has one page per definitive script, named after it. The custom-callout extension in _extensions/ provides the Rcode callout.
Each page loads its script with knitr::read_chunk("../R/<script>.R") in a hidden chunk and shows each labelled section with #| eval: false, with prose explaining what the section does and why. Pages link to the script on GitHub and to the scripts it depends on.
Never evaluate analysis code in the site. Pages render without restricted data.
Site-only helpers live in quarto/_site_functions.R, which pages source and main.R never does. They read only code or text given to them, never data, and are tested in tests/test-site-functions.R. A chunk calling them (for example side_by_side_diff(), which shows two versions of some code side by side) is the only other kind of chunk a page may run. Helpers the analysis needs stay in R/functions.R.
Function cross-references. R/functions.R has one top-level function per labelled chunk, and the functions page one section per chunk. Under each heading is the function’s name; after the explanation, Used in the analysis: links the method-page sections that call it, and Called by: the functions on the page that call it. Each method-page section whose code calls a helper ends its prose with Functions used:. tests/check-crosslinks.R derives all of these from the code and runs on every pull request; when it fails, run it with draft and copy what it prints, rather than writing the links by hand.
The original R Markdown file is shown on its own page as code only, with machine-specific paths removed.
The site renders to docs/, which is not committed. .github/workflows/publish.yml renders it on every pull request as a check and, on each push to main, publishes it to the gh-pages branch, which GitHub Pages serves. When you add a script, add its page and sidebar entry in the same pull request; render locally to preview, but do not commit the output.
Prose must match the code. If a change alters what a section does, update its explanation in the same pull request.

Outputs

Tables and figures are exported by R/tables.R and R/figures.R to tables/ and figures/. They are gitignored until they have been checked for errors against the published paper and cleared for release under the USRDS data use agreement.
Published figures need alt text.
README.Rmd is the source of README.md; edit the .Rmd and re-knit.

Restricted data (applies to everyone)
The Access column of “Data sources” says which sources are restricted. For each restricted source:

Never commit data, extracts, or saved objects or outputs derived from patient-level records. Keep data outside the repository, and check .gitignore before adding a new output type.
AI agents never read restricted data. Anything an agent opens, prints, or summarizes is sent to the model provider. Agents do not open data files or patient-level objects, print rows, or display identifiers, person-level dates, or small geographies (including ZIP codes linked to patients). Agents also do not open outputs from restricted data that are not yet cleared for release (tables/ and figures/ while they are ignored). Agents write code, review it, and run it on synthetic data; results on real data are produced by an authorized person.
No patient data to model providers. The cause-of-kidney-failure classification sends only the public $PD96DET code list. Never send codes chosen from, counted in, or filtered by patient data.
Synthetic data are built in code, labelled as synthetic, and never derived from real records.
Disclosure. Under the USRDS data use agreement, no count from 1 to 10 is published in a table, figure, flowchart box, or prose, including counts recoverable by subtraction or from complementary cells. Check every output before it leaves the approved environment, including scripts, comments, commit messages, issues, pull-request text and review reports (see R scripts).
Credentials and paid APIs. Never commit keys, tokens, or .Renviron. Ask before paid, bulk, or uncached API calls.

Coding conventions

Cohort flow uses the flowchart package, so the STROBE flow diagram and the analytic cohort come from the same code. Every inclusion or exclusion goes through fc_filter(), in the plan’s order. Never remove people from the cohort outside the flowchart. Record-level processing (choosing a person’s first Medical Evidence form, choosing the residence period that contains the dialysis date) is fine. An analysis that uses fewer people than the cohort (complete cases, a subgroup) reports its own number with that analysis. The cohort used downstream is the data from the final step (fc_view(what = "data")). Flowchart labels are built from constants in setup.R.
Code lists carry each code’s category, code system and version, and matching rule (exact or prefix). Check every code against the official code set. Never invent codes, variables, files, or definitions.
Joins use join_by() with an explicit relationship where possible. After every interval join and every join of records to people, assert that rows did not multiply, and decide deliberately what happens to unmatched rows.
Dates and windows are written as inclusive bounds, matching the plan, and the edges are tested on synthetic data.
Code that turns model output into reported numbers lives in named functions in R/functions.R, tested on synthetic data with a known answer.
Style: readable tidyverse code, following the tidyverse style guide. Transform data with dplyr pipelines (|>), one step per line; use stringr (str_glue(), str_flatten(), str_to_upper()) rather than paste(), sprintf() or toupper(); purrr (map(), pmap(), list_rbind()) rather than for loops or sapply(); case_when(.default = ) rather than nested ifelse(); \(x) rather than ~ .x. Select models, rows and columns by name, never by position. Checks are a filter() of the problem rows followed by stop() with a message that says what failed (or assert_unique() for keys), not bare stopifnot(). Long calls put one argument per line. Style changes go in their own commits.

Checks for any change
Check the items that apply before opening a pull request.

Plan: does the change implement the plan as written, and does it leave every open decision open?
Data sources: does it use the access package’s functions, and does their documented behavior match what the plan needs?
Cohort: do the flowchart steps’ order, denominators, and labels match their conditions, and can each count be reproduced from code?
Joins and denominators: no unintended row multiplication; missing, suppressed, and zero kept distinct.
Reported numbers: does each estimate match the plan’s estimand, and do tables, figures, and site prose say what the code actually computes?
Structure: is ARCHITECTURE.md current; are chunk labels unique and found by their pages; does every definitive script have a page and sidebar entry; does any site chunk run analysis code? Only the hidden read_chunk() import, calls to the site helpers, and results pages reading outputs cleared for release, run.
Execution: does main.R run in a fresh session with relative paths; are any saved intermediates or caches stale?

Project-specific checks:

Replication: does every difference from the original code appear in the plan’s section 12 and on the differences page, and is each one either a correction of an error or linked to a decision issue?
Geography and dates: are ACS, crosswalk and population matched to the year the plan specifies, and facility counts to the date of dialysis start? Are ZIP codes 5-character strings with leading zeros kept?
Denominators: is HSA population summed over the ZCTAs of the ZIP codes the crosswalk assigns to the HSA for that year, each ZCTA once, and are HSAs with no facilities kept as zero, not missing?
Area codes: are Dartmouth -88888 and -99999 codes missing, and are ACS variable labels checked for every year used?

Working with agents

Autonomy. The person directing an agent decides how much it may do, and may give it stricter rules of their own; those take precedence. By default an agent may edit code and documentation, add scripts and tests, run code and render the site on synthetic data, and commit to a branch and open a pull request.
Decisions. Anyone, including an agent, may add options and evidence to a decision issue. A decider states the choice in the issue. Agents implement decisions; they never choose among options on their own, in the issue, the plan, or the code.
Every agent, under any autonomy: never merges a pull request; follows the restricted-data rules; asks before running the full pipeline or making expensive calls; and shows a person the exact text before posting or sending anything as them, unless that person’s own instructions waive this.
Pull requests opened by an agent are focused. Each says which plan section or issue it addresses, what was checked, and whether by running code on synthetic data or by reading only. Synthetic results are never described as results.
References: cite the source documentation and literature used, in references.bib.

# Insurance hierarchy from the original code: none; else Medicaid; else Medicare

derive_insurance <- function(none, medicaid, medicare, advantage, group, va, other) {
  case_when(
    any_yes(none) ~ "No insurance",
    any_yes(medicaid) ~ "Medicaid",
    any_yes(medicare, advantage) ~ "Medicare or managed Medicare",

derive_nephrology_care <- function(nephcare) {
  nephcare <- str_to_upper(nephcare)

# 5-character ZIP code, restoring leading zeros dropped by spreadsheets
# (for example 501 becomes 00501). Anything else becomes NA.
standardize_zip <- function(zip) {
  zip <- str_remove_all(zip, "[^0-9]")

  case_when(
    str_length(zip) %in% 3:4 ~ str_pad(zip, width = 5, side = "left", pad = "0"),
    str_length(zip) == 5 ~ zip,
    .default = NA_character_

density_category_labels()
The labels of the five categories, built from the three cut points rounded to two decimals: 0, then >0 to the first cut point, the two middle ranges, and above the third cut point.
Called by: categorize_density().


Click to show/hide R Code
# Five exposure categories: 0, then (0, q1], (q1, q2], (q2, q3], above q3.
density_category_labels <- function(cutpoints, digits = 2) {
  q <- format(round(cutpoints, digits), nsmall = digits, trim = TRUE)

  c(
    "0",
    str_c(">0-", q[1]),
    str_c(">", q[1], "-", q[2]),
    str_c(">", q[2], "-", q[3]),
    str_c(">", q[3])
  )
}

title: Functions
text:
Density categories
categorize_density()
Zero facilities is its own category; the other four are cut at the quartiles, each including its upper bound, as in the original code. It stops unless there are exactly three cut points in increasing order.
Used in the analysis: 6. Density categories: Categories.


Click to show/hide R Code
categorize_density <- function(density, cutpoints, digits = 2) {
  if (length(cutpoints) != 3 || is.unsorted(cutpoints)) {
    stop("Density cut points must be three values in increasing order.", call. = FALSE)
  }

  category <- case_when(
    is.na(density) ~ NA_integer_,
    density == 0 ~ 1L,
    density <= cutpoints[1] ~ 2L,
    density <= cutpoints[2] ~ 3L,
    density <= cutpoints[3] ~ 4L,
    .default = 5L
  )

  factor(category, levels = 1:5, labels = density_category_labels(cutpoints, digits))
}

title: Functions
text:
Density effects
density_effects()
Extracts the density terms of a fitted model with Wald confidence intervals and the number of patients the model used: odds ratios for logistic models, differences for linear ones.
Used in the analysis: 7. Models: Fitting.
Called by: density_odds_ratios().


Click to show/hide R Code
# The density terms of a fitted model, with 95% Wald confidence intervals, p
# values and the number of patients the model used. Logistic models report
# odds ratios (exponentiate = TRUE); linear models report differences.
density_effects <- function(model, term_pattern = "^density_category",
                            model_name = NA_character_, exponentiate = TRUE) {
  # Computed before transmute(), where the new `model` column would mask the fit
  n_used <- nobs(model)

  broom.mixed::tidy(model, effects = "fixed", conf.int = TRUE, exponentiate = exponentiate) |>
    filter(str_detect(term, term_pattern)) |>
    transmute(
      model = model_name,
      term,
      estimate,
      conf_low = conf.low,
      conf_high = conf.high,
      p_value = p.value,
      n = n_used
    )
}

Saving each provider’s answers
cached_votes()
Saves a provider’s checked answers the first time and reads them back on a rerun, so a failure in one provider never means paying the others again.
Used in the analysis: 2. Cause of kidney failure: Running, checking and saving each model.


Click to show/hide R Code
# One provider's answers, saved to `path` the first time so that a rerun does
# not pay for them again. `classify` is called only when the file does not
# exist; delete the file to ask that provider again. `classify` is given the
# path of a file for answers saved batch by batch (`path` with .partial before
# .csv), which is deleted once the complete answers are saved. The caller
# checks the answers (check_votes()) whether they are new or read back.
cached_votes <- function(path, classify) {
  if (file.exists(path)) {
    message("Reading saved answers: ", path)
    return(read_csv(path, col_types = cols(.default = col_character())))
  }

  partial_path <- str_replace(path, "\\.csv$", ".partial.csv")
  dir.create(dirname(path), recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
  message("No saved answers; asking the model: ", basename(path))
  votes <- classify(partial_path)
  write_csv(votes, path, na = "")
  if (file.exists(partial_path)) {
    file.remove(partial_path)
  }
  message("Saved: ", path)
  votes
}

title: Published results
text:
Notes on the published results
These are kept above as printed. Each is listed so that the replication’s outputs can be compared with what was intended.
Figure 1

The 14,380 patients labelled “Receiving home hemodialysis” are those the original code removed for having a dialysis setting (DIALSET) other than codes 1 and 2. In the coding of the time (format $MESET_CUR), 1 was hospital inpatient, 2 dialysis facility and 3 home, so the box is right: home patients were removed. USRDS has since changed the coding, and the replication keeps in-center dialysis under the current coding; see the differences page.
“38,708 eGFR <20 mL/min/1.73 m²” are patients excluded for an eGFR above 20 (or missing), as the original code describes. The paper’s Methods say “less than 20”; the replication keeps the code’s rule of 20 or below.
The 224 patients whose ZIP code “did not agree with a ZCTA” were counted by the original code but never removed by it; see the differences page.
No box shows exclusions for missing insurance or for a ZIP code with no RUCA code, although the original code applied both. The original code recorded the RUCA exclusion as removing 0 patients.
The counts add up: 3,416,330 − 2,571,864 = 844,466, and the 12 exclusion counts sum to 2,571,864.

Table 1
Each percentage was recomputed from its count and column size, and each group of rows was added up against its column size. Four percentages do not match their counts:

Tunneled catheter, >0-1.36 column: 135,574 is printed as 94.3%; 135,574 / 174,185 is 77.8%.
Commercial insurance, >0-1.36 column: 20,378 is printed as 21.9%; 20,378 / 174,185 is 11.7%.
Metropolitan, 0 column: 9,186 is printed as 39.5%; 9,186 / 36,947 is 24.9%.
Micropolitan, >2.76 column: 28,576 is printed as 16.0%; 28,576 / 210,690 is 13.6%.

Three groups of rows do not add up to their column size:

Rural-urban type, 0 column: the four rows sum to 31,547, against n = 36,947 (5,400 short).
Rural-urban type, >2.76 column: the rows sum to 205,678, against n = 210,690 (5,012 short).
Race, >2.76 column: the rows sum to 210,691, one more than n = 210,690. As a result, the White row sums to 558,365 across the columns, while eTable 1 gives 558,364.

The other group totals (sex, ethnicity, nephrology care, dialysis access, insurance and etiology) add up in every column. Seven other percentages differ from their counts by 0.05 to 0.1 points, which is consistent with rounding an already-rounded value. Men total 484,346, as in the abstract; the Results text gives 483,346.
Table 2

The Model 3 sample without albumin and hemoglobin is printed “n = 844 4656”; the Model 2 sample is 844,466.
Model 3, category 3, with albumin and hemoglobin: 1.04 (1.00-1.05) with P = .06.

This page lists every way this replication differs from the original R Markdown file of October 2023, which produced the cohort and Table 1 of the published paper (Hemmige et al. 2024), and every place where the paper’s text differs from that code. Each entry is one of five kinds:
USRDS variables are named as in the data (for example DIALSET); the glossary at the end says what each one is.

title: Differences from the original code
text:
Cohort construction









Original code
Kind
Replication
Effect on published results




The CONSORT table was kept by hand, separately from the filters. The RUCA exclusion compared a labelled factor with the number 11, so the table recorded 0 patients removed while the next line removed patients.
Corrected error
Every exclusion is a flowchart::fc_filter() step, so the diagram is the cohort.
Figure 1 counts; the cohort itself is unchanged


At least eight filters were applied outside the CONSORT table: the facility linkage, a second sex check, missing ZIP population, % White, % Black, % Asian and % Hispanic, and missing region. The income and poverty rows were labelled “ZIPPercentageFemale”.
Corrected error
As above.
Figure 1 counts


The residence period containing the date of dialysis start was found with a join that would duplicate a patient with two overlapping periods; the code printed a check that patient IDs stayed unique but did not act on it. Whether any patients have overlapping periods is not known.
Corrected error
A patient with no matching period, or more than one, gets no residence and is excluded at the “Residential ZIP code” flowchart step.
Figure 1 counts, only if overlapping periods exist


A ZIP-to-ZCTA crosswalk was intended, and counted in the CONSORT table (224 patients in the published Figure 1), but never applied: ZIP codes were matched to ACS ZCTAs as if they were the same. Residents of the roughly one in five ZIP codes whose ZCTA has a different number (mostly PO box ZIP codes) found no ACS data and were excluded at the “ACS ZCTA code data missing” step.
Corrected error
The intended crosswalk is applied: each ZIP code is mapped to its ZCTA with the UDS Mapper crosswalk for the year (zippeR), with its own flowchart step. HSA population counts each ZCTA once.
Cohort size (likely larger), ACS variables, HSA population and density


DIALSET codes 1 and 2 were kept, labelled “Remove patients receiving home HD” (14,380 patients in the published Figure 1). That was correct for the coding of DIALSET at the time, which Appendix C still lists as format $MESET_CUR (1 hospital inpatient, 2 dialysis facility/center, 3 home), so the original kept inpatient and facility starts. The coding has since changed: in the current format $MESET (2024 Researcher’s Guide (United States Renal Data System 2024)), code 1 is home, 2 dialysis facility/center, 3 skilled nursing facility and 4 missing, so the same codes would now keep home dialysis.
Coding changed
In-center dialysis only (“DIALYSIS FACILITY/CENTER”, code 2 in the current coding), which excludes home dialysis as the paper and the original code intended (decided 27 October 2026).
Figure 1 counts, possibly: the current coding has no inpatient code, and where patients who started dialysis in hospital or in a skilled nursing facility now fall is not yet checked


eGFR was restricted to 20 or below, and patients with missing eGFR were removed in the same step without being counted separately. The paper says “less than 20”; the published Figure 1 labels the 38,708 excluded patients “eGFR <20”, which reads as a label slip for “> 20”.
Paper differs from code
The code’s rule: 20 or below, missing eGFR in the same step (decided 27 October 2026).
None; the paper’s wording differs only for eGFR of exactly 20


ACS data and the HSA were matched to the year of the form (MEFDATE) and facility counts to the dialysis date (DIALDAT). The facility join silently required the two years to be equal, dropping patients whose form was dated in a later year than their dialysis start.
Corrected error
All area data are matched to the year dialysis started, the same year as the facility counts, and no one is dropped for a year mismatch (decided 27 October 2026).
Figure 1 counts; area variables for patients whose form and start years differ


The density cut points were the 25th, 50th and 75th percentiles across patients in the cohort, so an HSA counts once per patient living there. The paper describes them as “the median HSA-level dialysis facility density across the country … 1.95 (IQR 1.36–2.76)”, which reads as percentiles across HSAs. The published Table 1 confirms the code: categories 3 to 5 each hold almost exactly a quarter of patients.
Paper differs from code
The code’s rule: percentiles across patients.
None; the published cut points come from the code


Each density category included its upper cut point (> 0 & <= q1, > q1 & <= q2, …). The paper describes the categories as “more than 0 and less than the 25th percentile”, “the 25th and less than the 50th”, and so on, which would put a patient exactly at a cut point in the higher category.

The study period was set by the date of the form (MEFDATE), with no upper bound; 2020 and later forms were removed only because no ACS data were downloaded for them. The paper defines the cohort as patients initiating hemodialysis from 2011 to 2019.
Corrected error

title: Differences from the original code
text:
How much simpler
The original file’s data preparation, up to the analysis file, is 880 lines of code (comments and blank lines excluded). The same steps here are 423 lines across five scripts (counted the same way: download_public_data.R, prepare_patients.R, link_area_data.R, create_cohort.R and define_exposure.R), because the access packages do the work: usRds loads and labels the USRDS files and counts facilities by date, tidycensus loads the ACS, and flowchart builds and counts the cohort at once. The facility logic moved into usRds, where it is tested and can be reused by other projects.

title: Differences from the original code
text:
References


Hemmige, Vagish, Priya Deshpande, Keith C Norris, et al. 2024. “Geographic Dialysis Facility Density and Early Dialysis Initiation.” JAMA Network Open 7 (1): e2350009. https://doi.org/10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2023.50009.


Levey, Andrew S, Lesley A Stevens, Christopher H Schmid, et al. 2009. “A New Equation to Estimate Glomerular Filtration Rate.” Annals of Internal Medicine 150 (9): 604–12. https://doi.org/10.7326/0003-4819-150-9-200905050-00006.


The Dartmouth Atlas of Health Care. n.d.-a. Frequently Asked Questions: Hospital Service Areas. Accessed October 27, 2026. https://www.dartmouthatlas.org/faq/.


The Dartmouth Atlas of Health Care. n.d.-b. Selected Primary Care Access and Quality Measures, HSA Level, 2015. https://data.dartmouthatlas.org/primary-care/.


United States Renal Data System. 2024. Researcher’s Guide to the USRDS Database, Appendix b (Data File Descriptions) and Appendix c (Data Formats). National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases. https://www.niddk.nih.gov/about-niddk/strategic-plans-reports/usrds/for-researchers/researchers-guide.
Project documentsAnalysis plan Code

Scope and reporting framework
This document is the authoritative specification of the study’s scientific objectives, population, definitions, estimands and statistical methods. ARCHITECTURE.md documents the implementation, AGENTS.md the working conventions, and GitHub Issues the open decisions and implementation status. Neither file supersedes this plan.
This is a replication. The design is the one published in JAMA Network Open (Hemmige et al. 2024), and every choice the paper states is treated as decided and cited to it. The original analysis code (an R Markdown file from October 2023, kept in original/) is the second source: where it makes a choice the paper does not state, the plan adopts the code’s choice and says so. Where the code and the paper disagree, or the code contains an error, the point is marked Open and linked to a decision issue for the deciders. Each such point is also listed on the website’s “Differences from the original code” page.
Reporting will follow STROBE (Elm et al. 2007) and RECORD (Benchimol et al. 2015). The reporting map below links each checklist item to a section of this plan.

1. Objective
To test whether the density of dialysis facilities in a patient’s Hospital Service Area (HSA; the paper calls it a health service area) is associated with starting in-center hemodialysis early, defined as an estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) of 10 mL/min/1.73 m² or above at initiation (section 7) (Hemmige et al. 2024).

Primary hypothesis (stated in advance by the paper): patients in HSAs with higher facility density have higher odds of initiating hemodialysis at eGFR > 10 mL/min/1.73 m².
Secondary: the same association with eGFR as a continuous outcome; with density as a continuous exposure; within strata of race (White, Black).
Exploratory: the share of variation in eGFR at initiation explained by HSA and by dialysis facility.
Replication objective: to reproduce the paper’s Figure 1 (cohort flow), Table 1, Table 2 and eTables 1 to 3 from public code, using usRds and flowchart, and to quantify the effect of each correction to the original code.

2. Design
Cross-sectional study of incident hemodialysis patients linked to area-level data (Hemmige et al. 2024). The question is associational; no causal estimand or target-trial emulation is used.

3. Data source









Source
Content used
Release or year
Linkage




USRDS Medical Evidence file (MEDEVID)
CMS-2728 form: demographics, comorbidities, laboratory values, access, insurance, primary cause of kidney failure, eGFR
Release held by the investigators, covering forms dated 2011 to 2019; variable definitions from the 2024 Researcher’s Guide (United States Renal Data System 2024)
USRDS_ID


USRDS Residence file (RESIDENC)
Residential ZIP code and state over time
Same release
USRDS_ID, date of dialysis start within the residence period


CMS Dialysis Facility Compare archives

December 2005 to April 2025, via usRds::dialysis_facility_snapshots (Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services 2025)
ZIP code and date of dialysis start


UDS Mapper ZIP-to-ZCTA crosswalk
ZCTA of each ZIP code
2011 to 2019, matched to the year dialysis started, via zippeR (UDS Mapper, n.d.; Prener et al., n.d.)
ZIP code and year


American Community Survey (ACS) 5-year, subject table S0601
ZCTA population, % female, % White, % Black, % Asian, % Hispanic, median income, % below poverty
Each year 2011 to 2019, matched to the year dialysis started (Walker and Herman, n.d.)
ZCTA (from the crosswalk) and year


Dartmouth Atlas ZIP-to-HSA crosswalks
HSA of each ZIP code
2011 to 2019, matched to the year (The Dartmouth Atlas of Health Care, n.d.-c)
ZIP code and year


Dartmouth Atlas primary care measures
HSA ambulatory-sensitive discharges, leg amputations, diabetic eye exams, HbA1c testing, mammography
2015 (The Dartmouth Atlas of Health Care, n.d.-b)
HSA


Dartmouth Atlas hospital resources
HSA acute care beds and hospital FTE employees per 1,000
2012 (The Dartmouth Atlas of Health Care, n.d.-a)

USDA ERS Rural-Urban Commuting Area codes
Primary RUCA code of each ZIP code
2010 ZIP code file (USDA Economic Research Service 2020)
ZIP code



Secondary-data declaration. The investigators have analyzed this USRDS release before: it is the release used for the published paper, and the published results are known. Every result of this replication is therefore a reproduction, not a new test of the hypothesis.
Data currency. The facility snapshot current on each patient’s date of dialysis start is used; a snapshot describes facilities from its CMS release date until the day before the next release.

4. Study population
Source population: every patient with a CMS-2728 Medical Evidence form in the USRDS.
Index event: start of regular chronic dialysis (DIALDAT) on the patient’s first Medical Evidence form.
Eligibility, in order. Each step is one box of the cohort flowchart. Steps 1 to 9 come from the paper and the original code; steps 10 to 16 are linkage and completeness requirements from the original code.

First Medical Evidence form per patient (earliest MEFDATE); later forms describe a second or later dialysis episode.
Dialysis started (DIALDAT) 2011 to 2019, as the paper states. The paper starts in 2011 because of the IDEAL trial (Cooper et al. 2010). The original code used the year of the form (MEFDATE), applying the lower bound explicitly and the upper bound only implicitly, through the ACS linkage (decided by Vagish Hemmige, 27 October 2026).
Age 18 or older at incidence (INC_AGE).
Hemodialysis as the primary type of dialysis (DIALTYP = hemodialysis).
In-center dialysis: DIALSET “Dialysis facility/center”. The paper excludes patients who began home dialysis. The original code kept codes 1 and 2, which excluded home dialysis in the coding of the time (Appendix C format $MESET_CUR: 1 hospital inpatient, 2 dialysis facility/center, 3 home; 14,380 patients excluded in the published Figure 1). The current coding (format $MESET, 2024 Researcher’s Guide) has 1 = home and 2 = dialysis facility/center, so the replication keeps code 2 only, the same intent in the current coding (decided by Vagish Hemmige, 27 October 2026).
Insurance status recorded (at least one coverage field marked yes).
Vascular access type at first outpatient dialysis recorded (ACCESSTYPE not unknown).
Sex recorded.
eGFR at initiation recorded and no higher than 20 mL/min/1.73 m², as in the original code (decided by Vagish Hemmige, 27 October 2026, in a working session: “Use the code”). The paper says “less than 20”, and its Figure 1 labels the 38,708 excluded patients “eGFR <20”. As in the original code, missing eGFR is removed in the same step.
A residential ZIP code in effect on the date of dialysis start (RESIDENC period containing DIALDAT), unique per patient.
The ZIP code has a ZCTA in the UDS Mapper crosswalk for the year dialysis started, and ACS data are available for that ZCTA and year. The original code intended this crosswalk but never applied it, matching ZIP codes to ZCTAs directly; the replication applies it (decided by Vagish Hemmige, 27 October 2026, in a working session: “I intended at some point to cross-walk this but never did”).
A facility snapshot current on the date of dialysis start. The original code’s facility join also required the year of the form to match the year dialysis started; the replication drops that requirement (see “Year of linkage” below).
An HSA for the ZIP code in the crosswalk for the year dialysis started.
Residence in the 48 contiguous states or the District of Columbia (excludes Alaska, Hawaii, territories, and states not assigned a Census region).
Race recorded (not unknown) and Hispanic ethnicity recorded (not unknown).
ZIP code has a RUCA code other than 99 (zero-population ZIP code) and complete ACS covariates.

The original code applied several of these filters outside its CONSORT table, and its table misreported others; see section 12. In this replication every exclusion is a flowchart step, so the diagram reproduces the cohort exactly.
Year of linkage. All area data (ZCTA crosswalk, ACS, HSA, HSA population) are matched to the year dialysis started (DIALDAT), the same year as the facility counts. The original code matched area data to the year of the Medical Evidence form (MEFDATE) and its facility join silently required the two years to be equal; the replication corrects this (decided by Vagish Hemmige, 27 October 2026).

5. Exposure
HSA dialysis facility density: the number of dialysis facilities in the patient’s HSA on the date of dialysis start, divided by the HSA’s population, times 100,000 (Hemmige et al. 2024).

Facilities: every facility listed in the CMS release current on the date of dialysis start (usRds::add_dialysis_facility_counts()), assigned to an HSA by its ZIP code and the crosswalk for that calendar year. Facilities whose ZIP code has no HSA are not counted.
HSA population: the ACS total population of the ZCTAs of the ZIP codes in the HSA, using the Dartmouth and ZCTA crosswalks and ACS for the year dialysis started. Each ZCTA is counted once per HSA, because several ZIP codes can share a ZCTA. ZCTAs without ACS data contribute nothing.
Categories: 0 facilities; then cut at the 25th, 50th and 75th percentiles of density among all patients in the final cohort (zeros included), each category including its upper bound. The paper reports cut points of 1.36, 1.95 and 2.76 per 100,000 (Hemmige et al. 2024).
Continuous version: density per 100,000, for sensitivity analyses.
Also described: facility stations per 100,000, and for-profit and non-profit facility counts.

6. Covariates
All patient covariates are measured on the first Medical Evidence form, at initiation. Area covariates are fixed for the patient’s ZIP code or HSA as described in section 3.







Covariate
Definition




Age
INC_AGE, years


Sex
SEX


Race
RACE (format $MERACE), reported in the paper’s five groups: White, Black, Asian, Native American, Pacific Islander. The five published counts sum to each column’s total, so the form’s Middle Eastern, South Asian and Other/multiracial codes were merged into those groups in the Stata analysis; how is not recorded. Here Middle Eastern counts as White and South Asian as Asian (1997 OMB race standard), and Other/multiracial as White, the largest group (chosen for this demonstration at Vagish Hemmige’s request, 27 October 2026).


Hispanic ethnicity
ETHN: Hispanic (codes 1, 2, 5) vs non-Hispanic (code 3)


Year
Year dialysis started (DIALDAT), “year of hemodialysis initiation” in the paper; the original R code used the year of MEFDATE (decided by Vagish Hemmige, 27 October 2026)


Comorbidities
Heart failure (COMO_CHF); coronary disease (COMO_ASHD); diabetes (any of COMO_DM_INS, COMO_DM_ORAL, COMO_DM_NOMEDS, COMO_DM_RET); cerebrovascular disease (COMO_CVATIA); cancer (COMO_CANC); alcohol or drug dependence (COMO_ALCHO, COMO_DRUG); immobility (COMO_INAMB, COMO_NEEDASST, COMO_INTRANS); institutionalized (COMO_INST, COMO_INST_AL, COMO_INST_NURS, COMO_INST_OTH). Each is “yes” when any listed field is yes


Access type
ACCESSTYPE: AV fistula, AV graft, catheter, other


Access to pre-kidney-failure nephrology care
NEPHCARE: none, some, unknown (unknown or blank kept as its own level), as in the paper’s Table 1 and the Model 3 footnote (decided by Vagish Hemmige, 27 October 2026, in a working session). The duration (NEPHCARERANGE) is not used.


Insurance
Hierarchy as in the original code: none; else Medicaid (including dual eligibility); else Medicare or Medicare Advantage; else employer group; else other (including VA)


Serum albumin, hemoglobin
ALBUM (g/dL), HEGLB (g/dL)


Primary cause of kidney failure
PDIS mapped to six categories: diabetes; hypertension and cardiac disease; glomerulonephritis; hereditary or polycystic kidney disease; transplant failure or complications; other (including unknown and unmapped codes). The mapping is described below (D4, decided by Vagish Hemmige, 30 October 2026)


ZIP code poverty, % Black residents
ACS S0601, for the ZIP code’s ZCTA and the year dialysis started


Rural-urban type
Primary RUCA code grouped as metropolitan (1 to 3), micropolitan (4 to 6), small town (7 to 9) and rural (10) (USDA Economic Research Service 2020), the four groups in the paper’s Table 1


Census region
From the residence state


HSA quality benchmarks
Ambulatory-sensitive discharges per 1,000 enrollees; percentage of diabetic enrollees with an eye exam (2015) and with HbA1c testing (2015); percentage of women with a mammogram in 2 years; leg amputations per 1,000 (The Dartmouth Atlas of Health Care, n.d.-b). Hospital beds and FTE employees per 1,000 (The Dartmouth Atlas of Health Care, n.d.-a) are described but not in the models. Dartmouth codes -88888 and -99999 are set to missing; the original code turned them into positive values (decided by Vagish Hemmige, 27 October 2026, in a working session).



Cause of kidney failure mapping. The original mapping spreadsheet is no longer available. The replacement maps every code of USRDS format $PD96DET (United States Renal Data System 2024), a public list of about 445 ICD-9 and ICD-10 codes with descriptions, to the six categories above. Three cloud large language models, called through ellmer (0.5.0 or later, the first version that sends current Claude models a native structured-output request) (Wickham et al., n.d.) with the same prompt and a structured output schema, each classify every code, and every model’s answers pass the same check: one each from OpenAI, Anthropic and Google. Two models run locally through Ollama, Alibaba’s Qwen and Meta’s Llama, receive the same prompt and are reported for comparison, but do not vote (decided by Vagish Hemmige, 29 October 2026): on the analyst’s laptop neither produced a complete, valid set of answers, and IBM’s Granite, tried first, returned none. A code is accepted when at least two of the three cloud models agree (decided by Vagish Hemmige, 29 October 2026; the rule was three of five while the local models voted, and was chosen because the classification demonstrates the method rather than being the main analysis); codes so accepted are not read by a person, and every other code is reviewed by the deciders, who record the category and their initials (reviewer). Agreement among the models is reported with Fleiss’ kappa in a one-row public summary (references/esrd-cause-agreement.csv), together with the number of codes accepted unanimously, by majority only and not at all; kappa is descriptive and plays no part in accepting codes. A second public file (references/esrd-cause-local-models.csv) reports, for each local model, how many codes it answered, left unanswered or answered with text that is not a code, and how often it agreed with the accepted category. The reviewed mapping is committed to references/ and is the only version the analysis reads. No patient data are given to any model; the local models send nothing over the internet. Patient-level cross-checks against USRDS’s own disease group (DISGRPC, PATIENTS file) and against the published Table 1 counts are run by an authorized person. The prompt defines each category in words, starting from the 12 groups of the 2015 CMS-2728 list of primary causes (Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services 2015) and the original spreadsheet’s sheet names: glomerulonephritis includes secondary glomerulonephritis (lupus nephritis, ANCA vasculitis, anti-GBM disease, Henoch-Schönlein purpura) and infection-related glomerular disease (post-infectious glomerulonephritis, HIV-associated nephropathy, hepatitis-associated and cryoglobulinemic glomerulonephritis), while other infections are in Other (decided by Vagish Hemmige, 27 October 2026). HIV-associated nephropathy is thereby counted as glomerulonephritis, unlike in the CMS-2728 grouping, where HIV disease is a miscellaneous condition. The definitions are shown on the website. The mapping written on 30 October 2026 (prompt version 02ff2fbb; 423 codes unanimous, 22 accepted by two of three, none without a majority) is accepted for the replication as drafted, with no changes after review (decided by Vagish Hemmige, 30 October 2026; D4).

7. Outcome
Primary: eGFR at initiation (GFR_EPI, CKD-EPI creatinine equation (Levey et al. 2009) as calculated by USRDS, with the race coefficient) of 10 or above vs below 10 mL/min/1.73 m², as in the original code’s GFR_DICH (decided by Vagish Hemmige, 27 October 2026, in a working session: “Use the code”). The paper describes the outcome as greater than 10 vs at most 10 (Hemmige et al. 2024); the two differ only for patients at exactly 10.
Secondary: eGFR as a continuous variable.
There is no follow-up; the outcome is measured at the index event.

8. Statistical analysis
Descriptive analysis. Table 1 by the five density categories: means (SD) for continuous variables and counts (%) for categorical ones, with classical one-way ANOVA for continuous variables, as the paper says (R’s oneway.test() with var.equal = TRUE; its default is Welch’s test; decided by Vagish Hemmige, 28 October 2026), and chi-squared tests for categorical variables. The paper lists one-way ANOVA, Kruskal-Wallis and chi-squared tests without saying which variable used which (Hemmige et al. 2024); Kruskal-Wallis is not used here. Missing data are reported for each variable.
Primary model. Mixed-effects logistic regression of eGFR ≥ 10 on the density category (reference: 0 facilities), with a random intercept for HSA, progressively adjusted (Hemmige et al. 2024):

Model 1: age, sex, race, Hispanic ethnicity, year.
Model 2: Model 1 plus heart failure, coronary disease, diabetes, cerebrovascular disease, alcohol or drug dependence, immobility, institutionalized, access type, primary cause of kidney failure, and (in the first version) serum albumin and hemoglobin.
Model 3: Model 2 plus insurance, access to nephrology care (none, some, unknown), rural-urban type, ZIP code poverty, ZIP code % Black, and HSA quality benchmarks.

Models 2 and 3 are fit twice, with and without albumin and hemoglobin; with them, the analysis uses complete cases (the paper reports 533,375 patients). The paper used Stata; its exact covariate coding and estimation options are not available, so these models are rebuilt from the paper’s text and Table 2 footnotes. Census region is not a covariate: the original code’s exploratory models adjusted for it, but the footnotes do not list it (decided by Vagish Hemmige, 28 October 2026, to follow the footnotes). The “HSA quality benchmarks” in Model 3 are taken to be the three the Methods give as examples (“such as”): HbA1c testing and eye examinations among enrollees with diabetes, and ambulatory-sensitive discharges. Estimation uses glmmTMB (Brooks et al. 2017) with the Laplace approximation; on synthetic data it matched a fully converged lme4::glmer about thirty times faster, and 7-point quadrature (Stata’s default) changed estimates only in the third decimal (decided by Vagish Hemmige, 27 October 2026). The linear models of eTable 3 also use glmmTMB; the variance decomposition uses lme4::lmer (Bates et al. 2015).
Variance decomposition. Null mixed linear models of continuous eGFR with a random intercept for HSA, and with HSA and dialysis facility (PROVUSRD) nested, report the share of variance at each level. Both models are fit on the same patients, those with a facility ID, so the shares are comparable (decided by Vagish Hemmige, 28 October 2026).
Effect modification. Models stratified by race (White, Black) (Hemmige et al. 2024).
Multiplicity. None; a single primary comparison is reported, as in the paper.
Missing data. Complete-case analysis for each model, plus multiple imputation of albumin and hemoglobin, which the paper describes as “a multiple imputation technique with chained predictive analytics (10 imputations)” (eTable 2), read here as chained equations. Only albumin and hemoglobin are imputed, by predictive mean matching, from the outcome, the density category and the Model 3 covariates, without HSA; estimates are pooled by Rubin’s rules. This imputation model was confirmed by Vagish Hemmige, 28 October 2026 (D7).
Software. R, with usRds (Hemmige 2026), flowchart (Satorra et al. 2026), tidycensus (Walker and Herman, n.d.), glmmTMB (Brooks et al. 2017), lme4 (Bates et al. 2015) and ellmer (Wickham et al., n.d.). The usRds version or commit is recorded with every result.

9. Sensitivity analyses







Analysis
Assumption it tests




Exclude HSAs with 0 facilities (reference: category 2); Table 2, Models 1–3 without albumin and hemoglobin
That distance to care in HSAs without facilities does not drive the association


Stratified by race, White and Black; eTable 1, Models 1–3 with albumin and hemoglobin
That the association holds within each race group


Density as a continuous exposure; eTable 2, Models 1–3 with and without albumin and hemoglobin, with them imputed, and by race
That the association does not depend on the choice of cut points


Continuous eGFR as the outcome (linear mixed model); eTable 3, Models 1–3 with albumin and hemoglobin, with and without HSAs with 0 facilities
That the association does not depend on the threshold of 10


Multiple imputation of albumin and hemoglobin (eTable 2)
That complete-case results are not biased by missing laboratory values


Excluding eGFR of 5 or below (from the original R code; not in the paper)
That results are not driven by implausibly low eGFR values


Each correction listed in section 12, applied one at a time
How much each correction to the original code changes the published estimates

10. Disclosure control
USRDS data are used under the investigators’ data use agreement. No cell, flowchart box or table entry with a count from 1 to 10 is published, including counts recoverable by subtraction. Tables and figures from USRDS data stay out of the repository until they have been checked for errors and cleared for release.

11. Limitations to address in reporting
The limitations in the paper apply (Hemmige et al. 2024). Specific to the replication: the cause-of-kidney-failure mapping is rebuilt rather than recovered; Stata models are re-estimated in R; and public source files (CMS, Dartmouth, ERS, ACS) are re-downloaded and may have been revised since the original analysis.

12. Corrections to the original code
Each is applied in the replication and its effect is reported (section 9). Decisions that belong to the deciders are linked.







Original behavior
Correction




A patient with two residence periods covering the dialysis start date would have been duplicated (a uniqueness check was printed but not enforced)

title: Clinical background
text: There is no formal eGFR threshold below which maintenance hemodialysis should begin. Most nephrologists use the estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) as a major factor, together with clinical signs and symptoms, the availability of dialysis access, and patient preference (Hemmige et al. 2024). The IDEAL trial randomized adults with progressive chronic kidney disease to start dialysis at an estimated GFR of 10 to 14 mL/min (early) or 5 to 7 mL/min (late), and found no survival benefit from starting early (Cooper et al. 2010). After its publication in 2010, the trend toward earlier initiation reversed (Hemmige et al. 2024), which is why the cohort here begins in 2011.

title: Clinical background
text:
Why facility density
If eGFR alone does not dictate when dialysis starts, the surrounding health system may. The hypothesis of the paper is that areas organized around high-intensity treatment of end-stage disease, with many dialysis facilities per resident, start dialysis earlier than areas oriented toward prevention (Hemmige et al. 2024). The unit is the Dartmouth Atlas Hospital Service Area (HSA): a group of ZIP codes whose residents get most of their hospital care locally, about 3,400 in the US (The Dartmouth Atlas of Health Care, n.d.-a). The paper calls these “health service areas”; this site keeps the abbreviation HSA.

title: Clinical background
text:
The measures

eGFR at initiation is calculated by the USRDS from the serum creatinine reported on the CMS-2728 Medical Evidence form, using the CKD-EPI equation (Levey et al. 2009) with the race coefficient, because that is the value physicians saw when deciding. The paper’s Methods call it “CKD-EPI equation 2012”; see the differences page.
Facility density counts the dialysis facilities listed by CMS in the patient’s HSA on the date dialysis started, per 100,000 residents (Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services 2025).
Area characteristics come from the American Community Survey (Walker and Herman, n.d.), the USDA rural-urban commuting area codes (USDA Economic Research Service 2020), and Dartmouth Atlas primary care and hospital measures (The Dartmouth Atlas of Health Care, n.d.-c, n.d.-b).

title: Clinical background
text:
The eGFR thresholds
Three eGFR values, all in mL/min/1.73 m², shape the analysis:

20, the cohort’s ceiling. Patients starting above it are excluded, because the paper restricts to the range nephrologists target for starting dialysis (Hemmige et al. 2024). As in the original code, 20 itself is kept.
10, the definition of an early start. It is the lower edge of the IDEAL trial’s early-start range (Cooper et al. 2010). As in the original code, 10 itself counts as early.
5, in one extra analysis. The original R code also fit the full model only among patients with eGFR above 5. The code does not record why. This analysis is not in the paper.

title: Clinical background
text:
Race and eGFR
The race coefficient of the 2009 CKD-EPI equation raises the eGFR of a patient recorded as Black by about 16% for the same creatinine (Levey et al. 2009). A Black patient is therefore more likely than another patient with the same creatinine to be counted as starting at an eGFR of 10 or above. Black patients make up a larger share of the patients in denser HSAs (11.3% in HSAs with no facility and 40.6% in the densest, in the paper’s Table 1 (Hemmige et al. 2024)). The models adjust for race, and the paper also fits them separately for Black and White patients (eTable 1). Current practice uses the 2021 equation without race (Inker et al. 2021); the replication keeps the paper’s measure, because the question is how physicians acted on the eGFR they saw.
